A TRUE STORY.

*Where is the baby, grandmamma?" The sweet young mother calls Prom her work in the cosy kitchen, With its dainty whitewashed walls. And grandma leaves her knitting, And looks for her all around; But not a trace of baby dear Can anywhere be found. No sound of its merry prattle, No gleam of its sunny hair, No patter of tiny footsteps, No signs of it anywhere. All through house and garden, Far out into the field, They search each nook and corner, But nothing is revealed. And the mother's face grew pallid; Grandmamma's eyes grew dim; The father's gone to the village; No use to look for him. And the baby lost! "Where's Rover ?" The mother chanced to think Of an old well in the orchard Where the cattle used to drink. ' "Where's Rover? I know he'd fmd her! Rover ?' In vain they call, Then hurry away to the orchard! And there by the moss-grown wall, Close to the well, lies Rover, Holding to baby's dress; She was leaning over the well's edge In perfect fearlessness! She stretched her little arms down, But Rover held her fast And never seemed to mind the kicks
The tiny bare feet cast Bo spitefully upon him, But wagged his tail instead, To greet the frightened searchers, While naughty baby said: "Dere's a Ittle din l in the 'ater ;

She's dust as big as me, Mamma; I want to help her out, And take her home to tea. But Rover, he won't lqt me, And I don't love him. Go Away, you naughty Rover! Oh! why are you crying so?" The mother kissed her, saying: "My darling, understand, Good Rover saved your life, my dear— And see, he licks your hand! Kiss Rover." Baby struck him, But grandma understood; She said: "It's hard to thank the friend Who thwarts us for our good."

'The man who lends his influence rarely gets it back. A fool may have his c.eat embroidered with gold, but it is a fool's coat still. Stay not until you are told of opportunities to do good; inquire after them. A handsome woman pleases the eye, but a good woman charms the heart. She who will not reason is a bigot; she who cannot is a fedi, and she who dares not is a slave. Cheerfulness is an excellent -wearing quality. It has been called the bright weather of the heart. The groundwork of all manly character is veracity, or the habit of truthfulness. That virtue lies at the foun- dation of everything said. An old bachelor says, "It is all nonsense to pretend that love is blind. I never yet knew a man in love that did not sve ten times as much in his sweetheart as I could. . _profesaor, looking at hi § wqtehi "As we have a few nunutes, I shall be gla,-1 to an uestion that anyawer anY one may wish to ask." Student, 'What time is it, please?" 2 Swell, "I want you to make me a short coat, without tails or seams in the back. Do you know what I mean?" German tailor. " Yaas, yeas, I know vat you vant. You 7,^4- a strait-jacket." Tio;"' tite yoti tO-CiltZ P ld thf: 400 n; ...My rheumatism has gone. I rubbed my knee well with your lotion," replied the patient. "'Your knee? But you said it was your arm." Yes; but the exercise cured me." It is selfish to dwell on our griefs, as though some strange thing had happened to us, as though they were too important to be relieved, or it were a virtue to sink under them. That bereaveratut seems rather iSttnetiiied which saddens the heart not Slier and softens without withering it,—H. Rooker. A pretentious young yachtsman, who was boasting of his marine experience, said to his uncle—" You lands- men, who always stay on shore, know nothing about squalls " To which the old man grimly replied—" We don't, oh! Let me tell you, young man, that I've got a little grandbaby that can give you points about squalls every day of your life." One of these English devotees to Mammon once re- ceived a lesson from John Bright, who did not seem to pay to him, the possessor of the purse, sufficient homage. The rich man pompously said, "Do you know, sir, that lam worth a million sterling?" Yes," said the irri- tated but calm-spirited respondent, "I do; and I know that it is all you are worth.' It was growing very late, but the young man showed no signs or disposition to take his leave. After relieving herself of several yawns, the lady said, "You have been reading about the Greely expedition, haven't you ?" "I have; why? "And you thought so much about it that you fancy you are now in the Arctic Regions yourself?" What makes you think so?" "Because you seem to be under the impression that you are in a region where *he nights are six months long." He took his hat. It is somewhat singular that, although all persons are willing to admit that there are many things they cannot do and many things they cannot comprehend, very few are willing to admit that there is anything they cannot criticise. If criticism merely means picking flaws and finding fault, it is certainly an easy task, considering that nothing is perfect; but, if we are to accept the de- finition given it by the best authorities, as "the art of judging," a certain reticence in its indulgence would be highly becoming. AT AN AFTER-DINNHR SP/RCM—The late William Cullen Bryant was often humorous in his after-dinner speeches. At a dinner given in New York to Mr. Wm. Black, the novelist, Mr. Bryant responded to a toast on poetry by saying that, although the novelist has laid society under great obligations, the poet should not be forgotten, since it is to him that we are indebted for some of our most labour-saving productions. "What," he continued, in his gravest manner, "could be more useful, more winning, more worthy of being remembered than that immortal song "—here the audience held themselves in breathless silence—"beginning, 'Thirty tihys hath September ?' " Tim Moose IN THE PANTRT.—An old man used to say to his granddaughter, when she used to be out of temper or naughty in any way, "Mary, Mary, take care; there's a mouse in the pantry." She often used to cease crying .at this, and stand wondering to herself what he meant. She often ran to the pantry to see if there really was a mouse in the trap, but she never found one. One day she said, "Grandfather, I don't know what you mean; I haven't a pantry, and there are no mice in "nether's, be- cause I have looked so often." He smiled, and said, " Come, and I'll toll you what I mean. Your heart, Mary, is the pantry, the little sins are the mice that get in and nibble all the good, and that makes you some- times cross, and peevish, and fretful. To keep the mice out you must set a trap for them—the trap of watch- fulness." A Secas-r.—A committee from New York, composed of leading citizens, went to see President Lincoln, during the war between North and South, in reference to the conduct of it. After they had transacted their general business, and the committee were making their way to the door' one of the gentlemen. who presumed on his acquaintance with Mr. Lincoln to ask particularly searching questions, stopped up to him, and in the lowest tone of voice said, "Mr. President, I would like to know where Burnside's fleet is going." Burnside had just sailed with the fleet, but the destination was un- known. "Well," said Mr. Lincoln, in a very low tone of voice, "would you very much like to 'know ?" " Yes, " he answered he would. "Well. now," said Mr. Lincoln, "if I were to tell you, perhaps YOU would tell someone else." "No," declared the gentleman, "I will not." Then Mr. Lincoln, putting up his iace as if to whisper, said, loud enough for all to hear, "" He's gone to sea!" Gontoos CALCULATION.—I have been married thirty- two years, during which time I have received from the hands of my wife throe cups of coffee each day, two in the morning and one at night, making about 35,040 cups of half a pint each, or nearly 70 barrels of 30 gallons each, weighing 17,520 pounds, or nearly nine tons weight. Yet from that period I have scarcely varied myself in weight from 160 pound< It will therefore be seen that I have drunk in coffee alone 218 times my own weight. I arn not so much of a meat eater, yet I presume I have consumed about eight ounces a day, which makes 5,806 poirnds, or about ten oxen. Of flour I have consumed in the 32 years, about 50 barrels. For 20 years of this time, up to 1831, I have drunk two wine glasses of brandy each day, making 900 quarts. The port wine, Madeira, whisky punch, Sre., I am not able to count, but they are not large. In champagne I have been extremely moderate, as I find from my bills that I have paid for 53 baskets in the last 13 years, which is about one bottle a week, and this not all consumed by me. When we take into account all the vegetables in addition, such as pota- toes, Peas, asparagus, strawberries, cherries, apples, pears, peaehes, raisins, &c., the amount consumed by an individual is most enormous. Now, my body has been renewed more than four times in 32 years; and, taking it for granted that the water, of which I have drunk much, acts merely as a diluent, yet, all taken together, I conclude that I have consumed in 32 years about the weight of 1,100 men of 160 pounds.—Cor. div.p: 1 One should seek for others the happiness one desires for one's self. 1 Professor (to class in mineralogy)—" Ce,n you recall a 1 miner • al occurring in the liquid form?' Philosophical , ' student—" Milk; because it comes in quarts" "How are you getting on at school?" asked a parent ,of his somewhat inchlent son. "I got kept in again to- day." "What about?" "About two hours and a half." I A little girl, on being asked what God made her for, replied, "To wear a red fodder in my hat." Some older 1 persons seem to have no higher conception of their mis- sion. " An!" sighed Mrs. Ogilvie, superintending the clean- ing of the house, "If 'twere done when 'tis done—." "Yes," sighed Mr. Ogilvie, "Then 'twere well it were done quickly." Janitor (to his wife, who has hung the water pail on the gas jet)—" Bridget, me darlin', did Mr. Levystraus tell you to put this pail on the gas?" Bridget—" No, Pat; but he was after sayin' that the gas was lakin', sure." "I hear Gail Fisher, who left here a few months ago, is married and living in Indianapolis. Did he marry well?" "Oh, yes, he married well. He was well when he married." "No joking. I mean did he get a good start by marrying?" "Oh, yesne got a good start—he married a widow with seven children." A wag, of whom we knew, whilom, in a Connecticut Valley Tobacco Growers' Convention, offered a resolu- tion that the "use of tobacco ought to be encouraged in the public schools!" He broke the dead silence that fol- lowed with, "Gentlemen, why do you balk? If this is a legitimate business, why not push it ?"—Aclvance, Some amusement was created during the examination of the four candidates for the ministry at the Geelong and Ballarat District meeting. One of the candidates was a Welshman, and sometimes his knowledge of the English tongue partially failed him during his examina- tion. Very laboriously he was making his way through a proof passage, when the chairman, with a twinkle in his eye, told the young man from Taffy's land to give the verse in Welsh. What a marvellous change! Im- mediately the slow, almost painful utterance was changed into an easy, rapid, and musical version of the words that came with such a laggard pace in the more robust but less euphonious Saxon.—Spectator ( Melbourne). AN ANctuisr TEMPERANCE PLEDGE,—On the blank leaf of an old English Bible, which has been transmitted from sire to son through many successive generations, and appears as the property, of Robert Bolton, 8.D., and preacher of God's Word at Broughton, Northampton- shire, is inscribed the following pledge :—" From this daye forwarde to the ende of my life I will never pledge any healthe nor drink a whole carouse in a glass cup, bowie, or other drinking instrument, wheresoever it be, from whomsoever it come, except necessity doe require it; not to my own most gracious hinge, nor any the greatest monarch or tyrant upon earth, nor my dearest friend, nor all the goulde in the world, shall ever enforse me. Not angel from heaven (who I know will not at- tempt it) shall persuade; not Satan, with all his oulde subtleties, nor all the powers of hell itself, shall betray me. By this very sinne (for sinne it is, and not a little one) I doe plainly find that I have more offended and dishonoured my glorious Maker and most merciful Saviour than by all other sinne that I am subject untoe ; and for this very slime it is my God bath often been strange untoe me and for that cauSe, and noe other re- spect, have! thus vowed, and I heartily beg my good Father in heaven, of His great goodness and infinite 1 mercy in Jesus Christ, to assist me in the same, and be favourable unto me for what is past. Amen. Brough- ton, April 10, 1637.—R. Botrox." THE LANCASHIRE Distscr.—The dialect of Lancashire is a puzzle, not only to Mr. Booth, but to our own countrymen. The Government Inspector of Schools for North and East Lancashire goes so far as to pronounce it vile, and considers it a hindrance to the teaching of good reading. The exponent of the Lancashire dialect, Mr. Ben Brierley, does not deny that it acts as a bar to the progress of refined reading, but when a Lancashire boy or girl consults the dictionary to ascertain the proper pronunciation of a word, and finds that it is sel- dom correctly given by even educated men, what, he asks, must be the feeling? "Not many years ago," he says, "I had the painful experience of listening to a young clergyman's tendering of ' Othello's Apology,' which he commenced after this fashion : Mowst powtent. gamy e , and w Taw tad seignyaws, My vewy nowble and appwoved good mastavri, That I have tign aweigh this oh s man's7daughtaw Is mowst twue; twue, I have mawied haw; The vewv bade and fwont of my offending Bath this extent, now maw." l' I wonder," he asks, "what dialect had interfered with this young gentleman's education? I will be bound to say It WM not the Lancashire. Sat, 1115v6i3Ver, may be the correct rendering of the English language according to the notion of some of our collegians; but if they have nothing better to offer in place of the method of reading taught by Qi.lr `vile fucfathers; we need not wonder at the vile dialect holding its own. Uneducated Lanca- shire people, as a rule, speak more grammatically than the same class of Cockneys. Yet we do not hear of this being a bar to correct reading in London. To the ques- tion, 'ls this leap year?' a Lancashire man's answer would not be 'lt ain't,' It would probably be "It is no.' If asked, 'Are those pigs yours?' he would not say I 'They ain't.' His answer would be, if in the negative, 'They're not.' If asked was he John Smith's son and he I was not, his reply would not be, 'I ain't,' but more likely, 'l'm not.' How does the comparison favour the Londoner? In the manner of dealing with the letter H the Lancashire man is rarely found tripping, unless he pretends to be learned, and then he falls foul of the un- fortunate letter with as much misadventure as we find in the typical ' Arry ! "—London Society. Tun LANDLADY.—The avocation of a lodging-home keeper is, for many reasons, one peculiar to women. Not only are there various negotiations best accom- plished by a female diplomatist to be carried on in a lodging-house, as in all other houses, with the baker, grocer, milkman, cobbler, and laundress, but there is also somewhat to be done with regard to the lodgers , themselves. They must be managed. No one can do this so well as a woman. Being managed means induced to put up with imposition—in short, being humbugged. Suppose, for example, that your tea-caddy feels sus- piciously light on your return home of an evening— though you would hardly scruple to say to your host, "Who 'has been at my cupboard ?"—you would hesitate in even hinting to your hostess your conviction that you were an injured man—delicacy would restrain you. I But even should you be what is elegantly and appro- priately termed "too far north," and that weakness be a stranger to your nature, how would you brook the endurance of such a tempest of exclamation as the fol- lowing :—" La! sir; well, I'm sure! to think that any gentleman should ever go for to dream of such a thing for an instant moment! There's nobody in this house, sir, I'll warrant, would touch a thing belonging to a lodger. As for Biddy, poor girl! she wouldn't wrong the child unborn, as the saying is; she'd never touch a pin, not she; as for me, -I'd rather go without tea, or sugar, or cream, or anything from now till next Christ- mas before I'd borrow ever such a morsel, even if people wasn't no ways close! Why, sir, there's Mr. Dromgoole, him as lodges on the first floor front; he is a gentleman, he is, and has been a living here these four years, and always gives the servant a suvring reg'lar as the time comes; and his friends is highly respectable, and his eldest brother, as used to lodge here too, was as thick as thieves with the Lord Mayor, and be never once—no, no more didn't his brother, all the blessed time they was here together—never asked a single question, nor found fault with anything; no, and didn't look over a single bill, only to see how much it came to; nor didn't mind the prices they paid no more than if they was princes! I declare I wouldn't have such a thing happen for all the world; and if I was a-going to die this moment, as Pm alive to-day, I wouldn't mind taking my oath that all the time I've been keeping house, and that's ten years come Lady Day, no gentleman ever suspected such a thing; no more they don't now, I'm sure, for no gentleman would ever think of bothering, and poking, and looking, and lifting, to see if he'd lost a hap'orth of tea. But a farthing's a great matter to some people."— Having-thus added insult to injury, the enraged land- lady ,bounces out of the room, and slams the door after her, leaving you to wish you had swallowed your loss, and she the tea-caddy and its contents together, so that your ears had remained unwounded by her oratory. .

AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS AND THE FRANCIUM—An interesting 'experiment is being conducted among the agri- cultural labourers of Wilts and Dorset. A series of mock ballots is being held, with a view t ) educating the new voters and of impressing upon tin m the secrecy of the bal- lot. The first has been held at Crondall, where a number of men were selected from the audience as voters, and Mr. Gladstone and Sir Stafford Nort6.cote were selected as the candidates. There was only one spoilt paper, and all the remaining votes were for Mr. Gladstone. Goon N.Y.—The death is announced at the age of 92 years of the Rev. Ed. Paske, who has held the rectory of Creating St. Peter, Needham-Market, which is of the annual value of £llO, for 66 years, and the vicarage of Battisford, Suffolk, which is of the annual value of £4OO, for 63 years. The deceased gentleman held the right of presentation to both livings. In one case the tetal population is 239 and in the ether, 435. These figures are supplied by Crockford, and it thus appears that more than £50,000 has been paid to one clergyman for the spiritual oversight of less than 700 persons during a period of over 60 years. cs.mk.ous Anemia, A. SOLICITOR—At Cumberland As- sizes, on Saturday, before Mr. Justice Day, Miss Armstang, a lady res;ding at Workington, sued Mr. Tom Wilburn, a solicitor of that town, for damages for professional negli- gence. The plaintiff had some property near Workington which was compulsorily taken by a local railway company, and the value was fixed at between £6OO and £7OO by arbi- tration. The company, however, disputed their liability to take the whole of the property, and plaintiff has never re- ceived any money. This she attributed to the negligence of the defendant in not prosecuting her claim before it was barred by statute of limitation. The jury found for plain- tiff, and awarded damages £6OB. Rxrirs.—The following letter appears in a contem- porary :—" Our farm in 1850 was 14s. an acre, and was from time to time raised to 275. an acre up to 1877. Since then it has been reduced to 20s. an acre, and is, therefore, 6s. higher than 34 years ago. This is not a single case, but the case on most of the large estates, and as a general rule in both Ridings the rents are at least now 25 per cent, higher than in 1852; and I venture to say the produce of a farm, taking it all round, is little, if anything, more now than it was 30 years ago; and yet there is a general complaint that rents cannot be lowered. In the face of such facts, how can such men as Mr. J. Lowther, M.P., and other landed agitators, preach such twaddle, and talk of other remedies for the farmers. There is no remedy but a general and a great reduction of rents, which the landlords are making a stand against.—A NORTH RIDING Fenxine." hreoars o Darn:. 129:789: CLLEES UNDER TRH AGRICIILTIRIAL HOLDINGS Aar.— Under the above Act a good many claims have been made by outgoing tenants in Kincardineshire. On the Arbuthnott and Barras Estates the claims have been set- tled privately, as well as on several other estates. On Fasque Estate (Sir Thomas Gladstone's), on the other hand, the claims have gone to reference, with the result that Mr. Wallace, outgoing tenant of the farm of Bal- begno, has been awarded £9l Os. 70., and Mr. Smith, outgoing tenant of Caldcots, £43 18s. 4d. The referees were—For the tenants, Mr. Falconer, Cairnton ; for the proprietor, Mr. G. J. Walker, Aberdeen. Many tenants have lost their claims in consequence of being too late in handing them in. It is stipulated in the Act that any tenant quitting his holding at the first term of Whit- Sunday should put in his claim to the proprietor or his agent by the middle of the present month, section 7 providing that the tenant shall, four months prior to the determination of his lease, give intimation in writing of the amount of his claim, adding proportion of cost of carriage and application, reserving any other claim he may have for manure and feeding stuffs used between the date of the first claim being handed in and the time of his removal. _ _ _

MR. I. N. EDWARDS ON ENSILAGE.—The report of Mr. Edwards, a judge in the ensilage competition during : Smithfield Show week, says :—This being the first exhibi- tion of silage (to any extent), it will not, therefore, be surprising that each judge had his own notions of what constituted good silage. I therefore think it is only right that I should explain how I judge silage. (1) The substance placed in the silo should retain its natural colour as nearly aa possible; (2) it should retain Hal natural amount of moisture ; (3) it should have a plea- sant and wholesome smell, and contain a very small Quantity of acid; (4) it should he soft and pliable. The time occupied in fillin„a the various silos ranged from one to thirty days, and I think this will account for many of the samples being very dark, and more like hay than silage. I think that a silo ought not to be kept open longer than four days. Of course it can be re-opened and added to from time to time. The method of com- pression is very instructive, almost every available means having been used. The weight used in compress- ing the silage varied from 40Ibs. to 5601b5.-per foot, namely :—Under 501bs. in six cases; under 751b5., six- teen; under 1001bs., thirteen; under 1251b5., nine; under 1501135., eight; under 1751b5., one; under 2001b4., five; over 2001b5., four. The weight used in the remain,- ing silos is not stated. The cost of making the silage is very ,amusing, and varies from 3d. to 355. per ton. I think that there are many lessons to be learnt from the exhil-akoh of6-11age, and amongst them the follow- ing :—(1) That good, sweet, and wholesome food can be made from rough materials, provided it is cut before quite ripe. I think grass should be cut seven or ten days earlier than if you were going to cut it for hay. (2) That &greater pressure than 751bs. per foot is not re- quired, and that it should be a continuous pressure. (3) That it is quite unnecessary to use any eVenSiTe ma- chinery for compressing the silage. (4) That the ex- I pense of making the silage varies accardlflg to cabh per- son's fancy, but it in no case ought to exceed 3s. per ton. I am afraid that the greatest drawback to silage coming into general use is the cost of the silo and the means of weighing, and the sooner this impression is re- moved the better it will be for all. • I would suggest that each farmer should select one of tie brick build- ings board up the doorway inside with feather-edged boards, and make a window in the toil or roof for fill- ing. He will have a first-rate silo, quite as useful as if it had cost £200; and he will find that the best weight to put upon silage is close at hand, natnely, a few old boards and some stones picked from off his fields. If the farmer wishes to fill the silo from off his arable land, I would suggest that he should sow rye grass or trifolium, and cut it not later than the first week in June. Then plough the land, and in the second week of June sow it with maize. These two crops would give him at least 40 tons of good silage per acre. AGRICT7LTU9AL IMPORTS IN 1884.—There are several interesting points in the table of agricultural imports for 1884, as compared with those of 1883. We imported fewer oxen and bulls by nearly 60,000 than in 1883, and that there was a decrease in the number of animals from every country named except Canada, and her small increase is to be accounted for by the shipping of American beasts from Canadian ports. The United States and Canada together sent us over 8,090 fewer oxen and bulls in 1884 than in 1883. There was a small increase in cows, and a rather large one in calves, chiefly from Holland; but the decrease in the imports of sheep and pigs was considerable. Germany was the only country which kept up the supply of sheep, while there was a decrease from 93,863 to 60,898 in Canadian sheep, and from 89,083 to 30,786 in American- sheep. With respect to cattle, the decrease has not been fully made up by the increased importation of 'dead meat, as we received only a little over 75,000 carts. more beef in 1884 than in 1883. The decrease in sheep imports, on the other hand, is more than balanced by the increase of • 264,756 cwts. of fresh mutton,.chiefly from New Zealand, but also largely from Holland. Partly owing to the dis- astrous droughts from which Australia has lately suf- fered, the frozen-meat trade has been comparatively small from there, while the New Zealand trade- has advanced by leaps and bounds. In 1882 we received only 37,283 cwts. of fresh mutton from Australasia; in 1883, 104,714 cwts. • and in 1884, 303,203 cwts. Al- though Holland sea us more mutton in 1884 than in 1883, she sent us more still in 1882, when the quantity was 122,045, compared with 116,182 hundred- weights in 1884. The fresh pork imports show a small increase. Nothing is more remarkable in the returns than the falling-off in the receipts of salted and preserved meats. With the exception of hams, there is a decrease all along the line—beef, bacon, pork, and tinned meats. The figures for meat "preserved otherwise than by salt- ing," meaning tinned and potted meats, show a great decline. The imports of butter and butterine, cheese, and eggs steadily increase. The figures for corn and flour show a very large aggregate decrease. This is largest in the case of wheat, of which were imported 47,113,998 cwts. in 1884, as compared with 64,080,444 cwts. in 1883, and 64,171,622 cwts. in 1882. This is not , all gain, as the decrease in the stock of wheat in the country shows; but, unless farmers have sold much • more freely than in 1883, the gain to the country by the good wheat harvest of 1884 has been very great In the • case of flour, although there is a falling off in the imports , as compared with those of 1883, there is an increase over , the quantity received in 1882, showing the great extent to which flour, chiefly from the United States, has been taking the place of wheat. In 1862 the flour imports were only a little more than one-fifth of the wheat im- ports, whereas in 1884 they approached one-third. Next to the figures for wheat, those for maize are most re- markable in the grain tables. In 1884 we imported 24,794,624 cwts. of maize, as compared with 31,538,952 cwts. in 1883. This was a great reduction; but in 1882 we imported only 18,255,285 cwts. of maize. A decrease in the quantities of barley and oats has taken place, a trifling increase in peas, and a small decrease in beans. The decrease in the stocks of wheat and flour referred to above is only that reported from the principal ports of the United Kingdom. Probably the decrease in the hands of merchants and millers all over the country is proportionately great, and we may have to import extra quantities rest year to make up for our short foreign supplies of 1884. MILK FROM TRH CONSUMERS' POINT OF VIEW.—In a recent paper on "Milk from the Consumers' point of view," Professor de Chaumont, M.D., F.R.S., Professor of Hygiene in the Army Medical School, having explained the object of his lecture, devoted a considerable time to a technical description of the principals of dietetics and of the composition and nutritive properties of milk, show- in's that it contained all the necessary dietary elements, albuminates, fat, carbohydrates, and salts, in good pro- portion. Milk was a typical food representing all the substances necessary for existence, and they found the young thrive better on it than on any artificial food they could give them. That was an answer to the extreme views of some of their vegetarian friends, who would confine them to vegetable food.aatßut to provide suffi- cient nutriment for an adult from milk alone, it would be necessary to take nine or ten pints daily, which would probably impair digestion. Milk underwent change with great rapidity; and probably absorbed odours and infected material as easily as any substance whatever. The best means of keeping it was to preserve it properly covered from all sources of contamination, especially air which, more particularly in towns, was loaded with various mischievous organisms ready to start fermenta- tion of all kinds. Milk was sometimes unfit for food from the presence of blood and pus which probably came from some sore or abscess in the cow. This was not only a disgusting but a positively dangerous condi-

tion. The serious question for the public to consider was the adulteration of milk. It was said that chalk was used to adulterate milk, but chalk would soon sink to the bottom, and would thus make the. adulteration

patent. Wate,r was the chief agent of adulteration. In London this was euphemistically called "Simpson." Unquestionably it was added to a large extent, though the practice was less extensive than was the case some years ago. It had been calculated that in the metro- polis alone there was £150,000 paid annually for the water added to milk. The addition of water was not only a fraud but a danger: children fed on such milk were insufficiently nourished and would easily succumb to disease; impure water was also frequently used, by which moans various diseases were propagated, such as typhoid fever, and probably also scarlet fever and diph- theria. The practice of creaming milk also made the quality poorer. The milk was allowed to stand for & time till some quantity of cream had accumulated. This was taken off and the milk " elongated " by the:addition of water and then sent out to the confiding consumer. The use of lactometers for ascertaining the specific gravity of milk were apt to mislead, because after the cream had been extracted, a quantity of water could be added to the milk and the specific gravity raised. The lactometer therefore in registering that good Milk was being supplied might do so even after the chief 'propor- tion of its nutritive properties had been extracted. For- tunately for the consumer, when an animal became di- seased, its milk supply decreased. !But on the other hand it was true that milk was often sold which lied been given by cows in a state of chronic disease, parti- cularly that peculiar form known as tuberculosis. Some pathologists had the suspicion that this diseased was transmitted to the persons who took the milk, and some forms of consumption were attributed to it. Whilst not entirely agreeing with the theory, he advised con- sumers to adopt the precaution of cooking milk in sus- picious cases before using it. Sometimes disease was introduced into milk by the persons who performed the milking, when convalescent from scarlatina, and this was a state of things against which every precaution ought to be taken. What the consumer wanted, and had a right to demand, was the milk as it came from the cow. The proposal that some general system of milk analysis should be established all over the country in the interests of the public had been objected to on the ground that the staff which would be required to carry out the inquiry would be too expensive. He did not think so—the expense would be justified. If the stan- dard quality of milk was below what it ought to be, there should be some authority to prevent its sale. A com- paratively small staff of inspectors would be required if magistrates, instead of fining 205., would fine £2O in every case of adulteration that was taken before them.

ENSILAGE EXPERIMENT AT ROYAL BIRKS FARM, LYTHAM. What promises to be a very successful ensilage ex- periment is being conducted by Mr. T. Fair, J.P., at his Royal Birks Farm, Lytham. This farm is situated just beyond the bounds of the Park; it is about a mile from , Lytham, and is in charge of an able agriculturist, Mr. Ibison, son of a large and successful farmer under Lord , Derby in the St. Michaels district. The attention of ' agriculturists in all parts of the kingdom haslesp C-C!allY during the past two seasons, been directed to the sub- ject of ensilage, and a large number of experiments have been made by landowners and agriculturists. rhough the general irnpreSgiNl Of these tests is favourable, opinions are varied, and the question, so far as this country is concerned, cannot be said to have passed beyond the experimental stage. Many of the farmers of our district have had the opportunity of seeing for themselves what ensilage is and in what manner it is made. The first to construct a silo in the Fylde was T. H. Miller, Esq., who formed a silo out of a carthouso at the Home Farm at Pool Foot. The object of Mr. Miller was to thoroughly test the system, so that his tenants and other farmers in the district could, if it proved successful, introduce pits on their farms. Farmers are often slow to hake up improve- ments, and they appear disposed to wait and watch for the perfecting of the system of "fodder bury- ing." Another silo was made by Mr. Mercer, of Alston Hall, and a rich and nutritious produce was the result. This last season the experiment has been renewed at Singleton Park, and a silo has been constructed at the , Royal Birks Farm, Lytham, which is, in all its arrange- ments, a model medium-sized homestead. Mr. Fair had the silo laid down last summer. In general arrange- ment it is very similar to that built at Singleton Park. It is well known that capital silage has been repeatedly made in old barrels, and it is rightly reasoned, if suc- cess could be obtained in small cask, why not in what would practically be a large one above ground. The silo at Birks Farm was constructed out 0 the back end I of a cart-house. A thick foundation of cement was laid, bl'QkCn in the centre with a shalloW Channel, from the I ' end of which projected into the yard behirid art tton pipe and tap, BO that the juice COUld be drawn off at any time I if it was found necessary. 'rhe sides of the cart-house I were also cemented, presenting an even and air-V.aght surface. The door at the rear of the house was boarded ' up with tongued and grooved planking, and art hir-tight front being constructed, all was ready for the crop which Mr. Fair purposed ensiling. MIR chiefly con- sisted of clover, which was cut and placed in the pit, due time being allowed for sinking. All excepting two loads was put in more or less wet, and Mr. Ibison in- I formed us that whilst some was being taken I to the silo water was dripping from the cart tail. I Judging by the result a,t the opening, it would appear that too long a time had been allowed to elapse between the former and the final filling, and this is the only mis- take which Mr. Fair observed during the whole process. The top of the silo was closely boarded, and the weight- ing was by means of barrels filled with large boulders— probably the most effective and convenient method which could have been adopted. The barrels were hoisted to the platform in front of the silo, and they were then raised by an endless chain check hoist, and pushed forward to the place required. It would per- haps have been better if the hoist beam had been nearer the window, but the inconvenience was not great. The pressure on the silage was estimated to be about 801bs. to the square foot, and all being completed the silo was left. The opening was fixed for Monday morning last, and the result of the experiment was watched with con- siderable interest by Lady Cecily Clifton, Mr. T. Fair, IP, and a few others, including some of the farmers in the district. A number of barrels were removed from the centre of the silo, and the boards lifted. It was then found that the last filling of grass was not as satisfactory as could be desired. It was rather sour, and was not fit for food. The solid mass below was then pierced by the cutters, and it proved to be as good as was expected. A square foot of silage was got out and weighed, turning the scale at 361bs. Samples were then inspected by each person present, and Henry Kirkham, one of the farmers from Peel, anxious for a practical test, hastened with a hand- ful of silage to the cowhouse. He also took with him some of the best hay he could pick out of the barn, and • gave the cows their choice. Three of the cattle after • sniffing their new fodder devoured it with evident relish, and would not touch the hay. One or two others , did not, however, fall in love with ensilage so quickly. Examining the silage taken from below, we found that much of the clover, both the bobs and loaves, was almost as fresh as when put in. The silage generally was thoroughly compressed, was of a light colour, and had a very sweet aroma. The experiment had been a gratify- ) • • ing success. There was no doubt that in the centre of ' the pit the weight per square foot will exceed 381b5. Mr. Fair did not allow anything to be added to the ' silage. With regard to the preservative quality of salt ' on ensilage. the opinion of Mr. Smetham, the analyst to , the Royal Manchester, Liverpool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Society (an opinion in which Mr. Fair evidently joins), is that if a silo is properly prepared and made perfectly air-tight, salt is of very little use in ' preserving the silage. With regard to the cost ' it is believed that generally ensilage can be pre- pared at a less cost per ton than hay, and if ' it shows good results in the milk pail and in fatten- ing stock, it will, beyond doubt be an invaluable ! resort for farmers in wet harvesting seasons. . Some who have tried the system say that it is better to use ensilage than middling hay, but almost all concur L in the opinion that nothing can possibly beat sweet, ' well-get, herby hay. One most important point for dairy farmers is the effect ensilage feeding produces on ' the milk, and the statement that milk from cows ' fed on ensilage is being repudiated as unfit to use, pre- sents the question in a serious light. This part of the , experiment, it is needless to say; will be observantly ' crrried out by Mr. Fair. Complete records are" made of ' the milk brought into the dairy, and the wanner in which it is used. Each cow now has a small quantity of ' silage given daily, and Mr. Ibison finds that they relish it all the more if, for a few hours after being taken from the pit, it is exposed to the air. Whether the yield of ' milk will be increased remains to be seen, but, in the ' opinion of the bailiff, the quality is improved already. ' Should the expected results follow, there :will be justi- ged the observation of Professor Sheldon, who, in a paper read at the recent Milk Conference said: "It is probable that the physical condition of silage, should the practice of ensilage become general, will alter the char- acter of the milk produced in winter, making it more like that of summer. And it is the physical condition of silage its east digestibility that will be found to be its chief merit—and no small merit either—over dry for- age." We hope to give the results of the experiment on the cattle at a later period.

THE POINTS OF A GOOD DAIRY COW. In a paper read at the recent Milk Conference, on "The selection, breeding, and maintenance of cattle," by Mr. Jasper A. Stephenson, of Carlisle, there is given a capital description of the points of a good dairy cow. Mr. Stephenson says —"In: selecting dairy stock, indi- vidual merit, rather than hereditary descent or breed, must be the guide. For those who, in endeavour- ing to establish a useful herd for dairy purposes, have their first stock to purchase, without knowing , their history or having any opportunity beforehand of applying the tests recommended, there are certain ex- ternal points in the build and general conformation of the physique of the dairy cow, which, if carefully ob- served and studied, will guide the buyer in the choice of the right type of animal required for his purpose with almost certain success. The points of a good dairy cow have been well ascertained, there being certain external indications of the capacity for milk production, which

are as apparent to the practiced observer as are the signs of strength and speed in the horse. In old dairy districts, where the owners are in the habit of filling up the herds annually by purchase, they soon become so expert as seldom to be deceived. To write out all the marks that are relied upon as showing merit or demerit would be difficult, but some of the leading features of service in determining some of the main charac- I teristics may be stated. It will be seen how the I following points are connected with milk production, and may prove of practical utility. First, the animal must have a feminine appearance, or, as an American writer has observed, "a cowy look." The next thing to be noted is the digestive apparatus, particularly the stomach and bowels. A large and strong boiler is not more essential to the power of an engine than is a capacious and vigorous stomach to the production of milk. It is an axiom which the continued practice of old-fashioned methods makes it necessary to repeat—' A cow cannot make milk out of nothing.' If she gives a large flow she must eat and digest a large amount of food to make it from, and she must, therefore, be fur- nished with a digestive apparatus adequate to the task both as regards capacity and strength. When the diges- tive organs are well developed they give depth and breadth to the abdomen, and a somewhat wedge-shaped form to the body, which tapers from rear to front. A large stomach and bowels indicate an abundance of the fluids, a condition, as may be readily understood, very essential to a large flow of milk. Broad hips and depth and breadth of the lumbar region are also indicative of a large flow of blood to all the parts surrounding and connected with the milk producing vessels. 'Gaunt cows are small milkers.' A good constitution, which is most important, may be judged of by the lustre of the hair and brilliancy of the eye and horns, and Large heart and lungs, of which a wide and deep chest are indications; though the lungs should not be ex- cessively large, abnormal respiration having the effect of burning up the fat elaborated in the process of diges- tion, which ought to be given out in the milk. If too small, the animal may be a good milker, though neces- sarily feeble and short-lived. The capacity of the lungs is also indicated by the size of the aperture through which they are filled; hence large nostrils: and in the same way the size of the mouth corresponds with that of the stomach; the width of hips and depth of abdomi- nal region also indicating the capacity of the stomach and other digestive and assimilative organs. A broad chine and wide hips denote a large cavity essential to good milkers. The Milk Mirror or 'Escutcheon,' of Guenon, however it may have been ridiculed by those whose want of patience has prevented its minute and careful study, is a reliable sign of milking capacity. The appearance and disposition of the hair on the udder and adjacent parts, which is said to be governed by the lacteal blood vessels, when observed in connection with the other points just enumerated, will be found a most reliable aid in prospecting or estimating the milk yield. If the reversed hair, turning upwards and outwards, and termed the 'escutcheon,' extends from the tail downwards over the udder and well outwards on to the thighs it may, especially if accompanied by a good development of the other points already described, bo relied upon as a favourable indication of a large flew, If narrow in its lower parts the flow will be small. If the uppoil partj broad and smooth a prolonged if narrow 4114 irregular in flow may be anticipated; its upper part, it is unfavourable to a prolong! flow. The size and number of the veins on and near the udder are also a good indication, and will be found to corre- spond with the size of the escutcheon.' But, as these indications may mislead if taken singly, they ought always to be considered together. Large 'escutcheon' and milk veins, coupled with a small stomach, would be marked down very considerably, and vice versa. Keeping the leading indications in view, observation will soon enable any one to make correct estimates. The points alluded to having reference more particularly to quan- tity, it remains to be pointed out that with regard to the richness of milk, the appearance of the skin and the ' feel ' of the adjacent tissues are valuable indications. When the akin and especially the ear, is of a yellow colour, and sheds a yellow dandruff, rich milk is an almost certain accompaniment, and if the skin be velvety and oily, and the substratum of cellular tissue be also soft and loose, it is a strong indication, if accompanied by the other points, of rich product: ra making choice by aid of these external marks preference should be given to cows with small bones, fine and slender limbs, and tail fine at its base; the head small, narrow towards the horns; the horns themselves of a rich, bright colour, tapering finely, and glistering; small neck and shoulders, apparently long because slender, especially near the head; small eyelids, well divided; prominent eye; teats not too small and well apart, and withal a gentle, femi- nine 10010 •

THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY. CHICKEN PENS. Pens entirely of wood and glass are to be preferred; or the 30 inches next to the ground may be of wood, made to open upwards, with glass above, the latter fixed. That will will answer very well, if the coops are set well back in the house at night, or when shut up. But we prefer all to be of glass. In either case the lower part must be made to open, and upwards, sq as to allow the birds to go in and out when the weather is seasonable. It is always well to have a large window in the ends also, and thus from early morning to late at night, every ray of sunshine falling on the house must enter therein. We do not use glass nearly enough in our poultry houses, and the six-inch skylights or windows generally to bZ fouhd therein are useless for anything save making the darkness visible. The most effectual warming power is the sun, and, instead of shutting out its rays, we should welcome and use them in every way we can. In every poultry house there should be a large sheet of plate- glass, in the sides which face the east, the south, and the west, and, if the roof should be a gabled one, also on that side which faces any of these ways. If plate-glass is too costly, then a double sash of ordinary window glass will answer as well. Should corrugated iron be used to cover the roof, and it is one of the beat and cheapest roofing materials that can be employed, it must be lined with wood, as it is a vary rapid conductor of heat and cold. Consequently it is very hot in summer, , ' and very cold in winter. Such a house as this should be well built. If of wood, inch or inch an a quarter deals ought to be taken, and the whole well tarred outside, so as to make it as warm as possible. The breadth should not be more than 6ft., and in building this will be a wise plan to follow, as then the maximum of space is obtained for the coops, and a larger surface for reception of the sun's heat, than in a squarer building. Of course, if some existing build- ing is to be employed then it must be made the best use of that is possible. The floor should be dug out a foot or eighteen inches, and half filled in with coarse gravel or broken brick or burnt ballast, and this covered over with as much sand as will raise it three or four inches above the ground outside. This sand will serve one or two seasons, if it is raked over daily and dug over once a month, and forms by far the best floor that can be adopted Upon no account should brick or cement be employed, and if ,in already it will be better to have them out forthwith. They are far too cold for chickens. If it is intended to use the house for hatching or fat- tening also, a shelf, should be put up against the back iwall, say, three feet above the ground. Upon this the hatching boxes or fattening pens may be placed, though we should prefer devoting a portion of the house for the hatching operations, and having the boxes for the sitters on the floor. But if space is valuable, they may be put on the shelf, and with plenty of damp soil below the nest eggs will hatch out well. Each hen can then be lifted down in turn every day for a quarter of an hour's feed- ing and the cooling of eggs. In a chicken-house like the one described a coop may be kept for every yard of its length. Thus, if it is 12 feet long, four coops can be placed in it, if 18 feet, six coops, and so on. The hens will have to be kept in the coops, or they will fight with each other, but the chickens can be given full liberty either in the house or outside in accordance with tho state of the weather. A. Lopse of this kind may be employed either for rearing by meajo of hens or where an artificial mother or brooder is employed. It must be kept clean, and be ventilated, but the opening windows will give every opportunity for an abundance of fresh air. SEASONABLE HINTS. We have at last had a taste of winter, and probably if any of our readers have hens sitting trouble may have resulted; or, if they have been gathering eggs in pros- pect, there will be considerable difficulty in obtaining sitters. In the former case it will be advisable to remove the hatching box to a warm room, or some place where the outside temperature will not affect that within. Should any hen have deserted liar nest, the eggs need not be thrown away, even if quite cold. They can be revived by washing in warm _water heated up to 105 degrees, and then may be kept in flannel between a couple of hot-water bottles until a hen can be procured. Fowls should have better food now, and a little meat will be found a great help. Some aromatic compound in the soft food will help to keep hens laying and be a preventive against disease.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING

rt'scEs.—When these are put up for the purpose of defining the boundary or to protect the garden from trespassers those who erect them are, as a rule, uncon- scious of the valuable service a close fence renders in another way. It is possible for a garden surrounded by a fence to produce crops a week or ten days in advance of one that is fully exposed. This is due to the obstruc- tion placed to the passage of cold air currents over the surface of the soil. Dumb animals give proof that they ' are sensible of this when they seek shelter behind the fence oven when it is helpless to supply the protection , they desire. The most perfect fence is a wall, which is provided for most gardens on one side at least by that of ' the dwelling-house. Walls are, however, expensive, and we have a cheap substitute in a wooden one, the height , of which, as well as other fences, must be regulated by I the extent of the garden, the larger the garden the ! higher, with advantage, the fence may be. For protec- tion only, a small garden: may limit its screens to the north and east sides of the ground, leaving the south and west most open to the full influence of the sun. Dead fences need not be the eyesore they are, as they , can be clothed with vegetation. All bare walls of dwel- lings should be furnished with some form of plant if there is the smallest enclosure in front of them. If those about erecting cottage residences would bear this in mind and consult some practical gardener respecting , the plants most suitable, as well as the nature of the ' border, they would be amply compensated for the out- lay, which would only be a matter of a few shillings. Among the subjects used for live fences we may name I the Beech, Privet, Holly, common Laurel, and Thorn. ' For fair sized Igarden the Beech is excellent and is 'ex- tensively used 1; y nurserymen to provide a screen for I their plants, because it retains many of its leaves during the winter. The Privet does the same, and is most suit- able for the smallest gardens; it is sometimes planted in ' conjunction with the Beech. Laurels are apt to get naked at the base, and Holly is a plant that will:not thrive in some soils, otherwise it is most suitable, as it is well furnished with glossy green foliage all through the winter. The Thorn is too well known to need comment. For cottage garden fences we should like to see the gooseberry more extensively used. Farmers and others might take the hint and mix them up with the thorn, or confine them to one end for comparison. We feel sure they would be satisfied with the results, as the goose- berries may—in fact, ought to—be gathered green; to leave them to ripen would be too hazardous. In a green state they are much sought for by fruit preservers for bottling' so as to have green gooseberry tarts at any time of the year. Allotment owners would do good ser- vice if they defined the boundary of these by rows of gooseberry and currant trees, charging a small per- centage for their cost in the rent. As the plots are usually exposed, several rows of this running this way and that way would afford considerable protection to the young, low-growing plants in the early part of the year. During frosty weather seed potatoes, as well as those intended for culinary purposes, should have an extra protection. All seem determined to grow, and we have spread as thinly as space would allow us on the floor of a room those intended for planting; this will retard them considerably. Some of the forwardest of the Kidney we have stood on end with the most promising sprouts upwards.

Tns FRONT GARDEN.—Crocus and other bulbs will need watching, as in severe weather mice are forced to do what they would not in fine open weather. Frost locks the doors of their food stores, so that they are unable to feed from the usual source; hence they attack many kinds of bulbs, the Crocus and the Snowdrop being amongst the first. The latter of these are now peeping through the ground, and are either in great danger of being nibbled off above the surface, or the mice follow the growth down till they reach the bulbs, which they greedily devour. Traps should, therefore, be laid with- out delay. Cats may be persuaded to watch the bulb beds, if pieces of bloater or red herring are placed near to where the mice have been at work. This should be done at night, as it is most probable that when puss is attracted by the fish it will at the same time smell the mice, and lay in wait for them. If it does not on its first visit it may the second, for it is almost sure to return in search of more fish:

THE WINDOW.—The sweet scented leaf Geranium must be frequently examined for green fly, and prompt measures taken to destroy it as soon as it appears. This section of the Geranium differs from all others, as it is always in a growing state, and for that reason must at no time be allowed to get into a dry condition.

_ A LDERSHOT MORTI7ARY CHAPEL BURNT DOWN.—About half an hour after midnight on Saturday the Mortuary Chapel at the Military Cemetery, situated on a hill over- looking the town and camp, Aldershot, was seen to be on tire, which spread so qnickly that in less than an hour the building was completely gutted. From the rapidity with which the flames spread, the fire is supposed to have been the work of an incendiary. An innkeeper at Newtown states that he heard two explosions about twelve. All the registers are destroyed, and the bell melted. There is no fireplace in the chipel. A small fire in the Protestant vestry was put out when the caretaker left.

div.head: FATAL MISTAKE IN AMERICA.
div.p: A FATAL MISTAKE IN AMERICA.

Tte ae•.sland (Ohio, 17.8,A.) Press, of Feb. 23, 18-8?, pub- lishes an accJunt of a fatal surgical operation which has caused a great commotion among me:'ical men throughout the whole country, Dr. Thayer, the most eminent surgeon in Cleveland, prcnouncing it icandalous. It appi ars that a Mrs. King had been suffering for many years with some disease of the stomach which had resisted the treatment of all the physicians in atten- danee. The disease commenced with a slight deran.tement of_ the digestion, with a poor appetite, followed by a peculiar in describable distress in the stomach, a feeling that hat been des- ailed as a faint "all gone" sensation, a sticky slime collecting about the teeth, causing a disagreeable taste, especially in the mo rang. This sensation was not removed by food, but on the contrary, it was increased. The eyes then became tinged with yellow, and were tanked. After a while the hands and feet be- cameceld and sticky—a cold perspiration, There was a constant tired and languid feeling. Then followed a dreadful nervous- ness, with gloomy forebodings, When rising suddenly there came a dizzy feeling hire vertigo. Alter a time the bowels be- came costive, lo that it was difficult to procure a movement without a cathartic Boon followed a disposition to spit up the food after eating, sometimes in a sour, fermented condi- tion. All this derangement caused a terrible palpitation of the heart, so air to make the breathing difficult. Finally, the patient was unable to retain any fond whatever, and there was oonemnt pain in the abdomen. All prescribed remedies falling, to give relief a consultation was held, when it was decided that the patient had a cancer in the stomach, and, in order to save the patient's life, an operation was justifiable. Accordingly, on. February 22, 1883, the opera- tion was performed by Dr. Vance, in the presence of Dr. Tuckerman, Dr. Perrier, Dr. Arms Dr. Gordon, Dr. Lapner, and Dr 11411v/ell, of the Police Board. The operation con- sisted in laying open the cavity of the abdomen and exposing the stomach, bowels, liver, and pancreas. Whoa this bad been done, an examination of the organs was made, but, to the horror and dismay of the doctors, there was no cancer to to found. The patient did notolaave a cancer. When too late. the medical men discovered that they had made a terrible mistake. They sewed the parts together and dressed the wound that they had made, but the poor woman sank from exhaustion and died in a few hours. How sad it must be for the husband of this poor woman to know that his wife died from the effects of a surgical operation that ought never to have been performed. It this woman had taken the proper remedy for dyspeneia (for this is what the disease really was) she would have been living to-day. EGYPT AND THE SOUDA.N. -1388i0E8 FROM LORD WOLSELEY dr GENERAL GORDON.—FIGHTING NEAR KHARTOUM.—MORE TROOPS FOR SUAKIM. From Lord Wolseley r—" Korti, Saturday.—Large convoy .eeturned to-day from Gakdul. All quiet all along the route. 40-morrow convoy of Sowerab and Hawalvir tribes takes !tomato Gakdul. Saleb, the Chief of Kabbabish, has come la• He reached our post at Debbah to-day, and comes on L'ere at once. Oar English boats coming in. It is satisfac- TY to know that out of eight hundred landed in Egypt a4out seven hundred are now working along the river, and many lrzainder are now being repaired, a small number been totally wrecked at various times and Places." WITTY GENERAL EARLE'S COLUMN.—MERAWI, SUNDAY. -••••The preparations here for the advance of the column are Progressing rapidly. General Brackenbury - has inspected tila Egyptian artillery, and that portion of the Camel Corps attached to this division. After the inspection the latter ;°rPs who are under the command of Major Marriot, started ,or damdab, where they will be usefully employed in scout- the country ahead, and in learning something of the a,tlenber and disposition of the hostile tribesmen. The .1,,,31ack Watch are now arriving at Hamclab. The Cornwall gitnent are here, and will not advance for a short time. wheir boats, with all others disengaged, are at present /Ptallg up and down the river, transporting supplies to "arndab. ALExAteraRTA, SATURDAY. The Khedive received last bight the following telegram from the Mudir of Dongola : My messenger to General Gordon has returned. He "a3's On leaving Dongola I went by the desert to the village Zeziret Rocit, where I met a steamer, in which I Went to Khartoum. During the journey the crew of the .;.esael frequently fired upon the rebels, who returned the re• On approaching Khartoum the rebels fired from both aides of the river, but General Gordon sent two steamers to liaiet us to disperse the rebels. Thus we entered safely in- ,o Khartoum. General Gordon immediately questioned me Ile to the state of Dongola. During my stay in Khartoum 11; e Mandi sent a letter to General Gordon asking permis- koo to enter Khartoum. General Gordon replied that he cOld come, and he was willing to go to Oindurman to re- him. Orders were given to the troops to be ready. eneral Gordon, with four river steamers carrying cannons, .er°l9ed the river to Omdurman. On their arrival a con- aiderable number of rebels attacked them. A sharp fight place, and the rebels sank one steamer with a shell. tile other steamers rescued the crew and continued the 4ghl, eventually dispersing the enemy. The messenger rerwards visited the Mandi's camp, and learned that the slandi had several men kept in chains, among whom were tlea Eey,Makhi Slaten Bey, and many others; but Hus- le,,nl Bey was at Haifa free, and prays daily with the Mandi. lee strong tribe of the Bakarahs left the Mandi, and were !ellowed by his troops, but they fought and beat the 4abdi's men The tribe have returned to their homes.'" .13ERLIN, SUNDAY. According to intelligence re- celeed here from Constantinople, the Sultan has given Zers for an expedition of 6,000 men to occupy Suakim. 6 religious party at the palace are opposed to the ex- Pedition.

Sir Ralph Thompson, Permanent

Secretary to the War Office, was early in attendance at his official duties on Thursday morning, and immediately set to work upon the many telegrams which awaited his con- sideration. Lord Hartington was kept well-inforund throughout the night of all the news received front Egypt. The absence of further news is easily accounted for by the circumstance that Matammeh being at least five days' journey from Korti, and the route across the desert between those places being at pre- sent unsafe for travellers, it would be necessary for a small armed party to be sent as an escort to any bearer of des- patches to headquarters, and thus some delay will occur before Lord Wotseley is in possession of definite news of the occupation of Matammeh. During Thursday the War Office was able to communicate some information as to the state of the wounded officers. It was stated in answer to a relative of Lieutenant Lyall, R.A., that that officer was sinking fast. A telegram was received from Lord Airlie stating that General Stewart's staff was in the thick of the fight, and all behaved most gallantly. Lord Airlie was wounded in the hand, but was able to cantinue on flute. Several inquiries were also made at the Ad- miralty as to casualties in the Naval Brigade, which were fortunately few. The authorities iastead of publishing the list in their department, as is usual, sent it to the War Office. Frequent telegrams were deapatched on Thursday from the War Department to Lord Wolseley. All the latest intelligence received from Egypt has been com- municated to the Queen at Osborne. Lord Harlington, who has been in constant attendance at the War report- meat since the reception of the news of the engagement at Abu Klee, early on Thursday morning had a conference with Mr. Gladstone in Downing-street. Earl Granville afterwards visited the Premier. THE POWERS AND EGYPT.—REPLIES TO THE BRITISH NOTE. M. Waddington, the French Ambassador, called at the Foreign Office on Saturday afternoon, and presented the counter-proposals of the French Goviroment on the Egyp- tian financial question to Earl Granville, who had arrived in London from Weimer Castle in the afternoon. After the French Ambassador had left, the Italian Anabassador, Count Nigra, called at the Foreign Office and saw Earl Granville. Earl Granville attended early on Monday at the Foreign Office, where, between three and four p.m., be received several Ambassadors, each of whom delivered to his Lord- ship the reply of his respective Government to the British proposals for the settlement of Egyptian financial affairs. The replies of the Powers, though uniform in substance, display great anxiety not to say anything which could ap- pear like an intention or even a tendency to offend English susceptibilities. The Powers, notwithstanding Lord North- brook's report, deem it essential that an investigation on the spot by represertatives of the various Powers ought to be undertaken to ascertain the real state of Egyptian finances. They acknowledge the urgency of meeting the exigencies of the Egyptian Treasury, and also of the Indem- nities. But instead of England first guaranteeing £5,000,000, and next issuing £4,000,000, they suggest a single loan of £9,000,000, subject to a collective gaarantee. FRANCE AND CHINA. PARIS, SIINDLY.—A despatch from Shanghai of to-day's date, states that 12 Chinese vessels left that port yester- day. It is believed that they proceed to Foochow in order to embark troops, which they will endeavour to land at Formosa.

THE MURDER AT FRANKFORT. BRUSSELS, SATURDAY.—A suspicious-loeking man, who arrived on Friday at Antwerp from Germany, excited the susp'cions of the police. A vigilant watch was kept upon his movements, and on his leaving the town he was closely followed. On his reaching Brussels he was ar- rested on suspicion of being the murderer of Councillor Rumpff, who was found stabbed outside his own door last week. SWEDEN. STOCKHOLM, MONDAY. The Riksdig was opened to- day. The Budget is drawn up on the basis of a reduc- tion of 30 per cent in the land tax. No fresh taxation is proposed. FRESH EARTHQUAKE IN SPAIN. MADRID, SATURDAY.—Another severe shock of earth- quake occurred at Granada at ten o'clock last night, causing great alarm among the inhabitants. MADRID, THURSDAY.— Fresh earthquake shocks occur- red yesterday morning at Malaga Loj I, Velez Malaga, and Almnnega. The lattsr place suffered some damage. REVOLUTION IN CENTRAL AMERICA. NEW YORK, SUNDAY.—According to a telegram from Panama, the revolution has now extended to five States of the Republic. The rebels hold Barranquilla. They also captured Carthagena, which town was, however, re- taken. DISASTROUS AVALANCHE. VIENNA, SUNDAY.—WhiIe twenty persons were driving to market at Klagenfurt yesterday, an avalanche fell from a hill and overwhelmed them. Efforts are being made to rescue the unfortunate men, but have, so far, been with- out success.

BERLIN, SATURDAY—The DEWS from Paris to-day is to the effect that Portugal continues her opposition to an ami- cable settlement with the African Association. Considerable irritation is manifest among the Plenipotentiaries here on this account. BRITISH ANNEXATIONS IN THE SOUTH PACIFIC. MELBOURNE, VVEDNESDAY.—The Commodore of the Aus- tralian Squadron has hoisted the British flag on the Lonisi- ades, Woodlark Island, the iluon Gulf, and the d'Entrecas- teaux Islands. BERLIN. WEDNESDAY.—The North German Gazette to- day, referring to the news received from Australia that New Zealand intended establishing steamer communication be- tween Auckland and Samoa and the Tonga Islands, regards this as an intended attempt to counteract German enterprise, which has hithetto been paramount in Samoa and the Tonga Islands, and to gain a commanding influence in Samoa and Tonga. The inhabitants of New Zealand at all events expect an extension of British rule to the eastern portion of the South Pacific.

THE CONGO. LISBON, TIMILSDAT.—It is affirmed that Portugal, in the negoti,itions at present proceeding, has not yet relinquished any of her ancient claims with regard to the Congo terri- tory. MURDER OF ORANGEMEN. ST. Jour; NEWFOUNDLAND, THORSDAY.—Nineteen of the Catholics from Riverad, near Harbour Grace, have been acquitted of the murder of Orangemen in riots at St. Stephen's Bay. They were, however, recommitted on the charge of murdering three others.

LOSS OF THE ADMIRAL MOORSOM. The Dublin and Holyhead steamer Admiral Moorsom falsely reported to have put into Douglas on Friday, dis- abled, was really sunk OD Thursday after collision with a large American vessel, the Santa Clara. The Admiral Moorsom left Dublin with 34 souls, crew, and cattle drovers en board, and proceeded all well until a vessel was sighted, and Captain Weekes steamed under its stem. Then the Santa Clara was discovered bearing down upon the Admiral Moorsem, and a terrible collision immedately took place, the funnel, mainmast, and rigging of the Admiral Moorsom being carried away and half her boats destroyed. A small boat was launched, and eleven persona crowded into it. This boat at once disappeared, and was supposed to have been lost. The second boat was then launched, and by it ten of the crew and two passengers were taken on board the Santa Clara, and the.chief officer and the man on the look out had already leaped on that vessel. The second mate and a pas- senger endeavoured to do likewise, but lost their lives in the attempt. The captain of the Admiral Moorsom leaped or was knocked overboard, and the vessel then drifted help- lessly about, with three men, a woman, and a child, and the body of a man on board. The disabled steamer was seen by the schooner Peter James, which, however, was unable to render assistance and was taken in tow by the steamer Falcon, of Cork, by which vessel the men, woman, and child were saved. Subsequently the steamer Lady Wode- house took the Admiral Moorsom in tow on Friday evening, and two hours afterwards the doomed steamer sank, breaking the tow ropes. On Monday the welcome news reached Liverpool that the occupants of the first boat that was launched had been picked up by the Liverpool-bound brig- antine Stanley, which arrived in the Mersey oa Monday evening. It appears that the roughness of the sea immedi- ately separated the occupants of this boat from the Admiral Moorsom, and that all they could then do was to keep the bow of the boat to the sea and drift about in the hope of , being picked up. Several vessels passed them in the night, and it was not until about midday on Friday that they were rescued by the Stanley, on board of which they were treated with the utmost kindness. The fate of the captain is still in- volved in some obscurity, and it has been rather hastily in- ferred that he failed in his duty when the collision occurred. The survivors, however, testify that Captain Weekes was not the kind of man to give way to panic, and they believe be was swept overboard by some loose rt. ging of the Santa Clara, The number of persons drowned is supposed to be five, viz., Captain Weekes, the master of the steamer; Wm. Abbott, second mate; Mr. Wooldridge, cattle dealer ; and a soldier and another man, whose names are as yet un- known. On Tuesday, a communication was received in Liverpool from the BJard of Trade, o•dering the necessary steps to be taken for holding an inquiry into the loss of the Admiral Moorsom. Captain Dunn, of the Santa Clara, however, re- fuses to recognise any other than the American tribunal, either in relation to the collision or to an alleged stabbing affray on board his vessel, and so far be has declined to make ay deposition to the Receiver of Wre iks at Liver- po• I. Ile has nevertheless expressed himself willing to give evidence on any British inquiry, provided it takes place before his vessel is again ready for sea. The owners of the Admiral Mooreom have intimated their intention of bringing an action against the owners of the Santa Clara to recover damages. The reported stabbing affray on board the Santa Clara in Birkenhead Docks is denied by the ship's agents, who state that only a fight with fists occurred,

The visitors made a claim of "off side," however, and it was upheld by the referee. Im- mediately the game had been restarted the Crewe forwards rushed up the field and Done sent the ball through the Earlestown goal, amid inuch applause. The Earlestonians put in a claim of "offside," but the referee allowed the point, and Crewe thus scored their first goal. Half-time was then called and ends were chan- ged. Flaying with the ground and wind in their favour, the Crewe men began to press their opponents, and after ten minutes play Snelson equalised the game. Great excitement was now manifested on every side of the field. Both teams were 'cheered on by encouraging shouts of their supnortere, and the respective players put forth every effort to secure a leading point. The visitors had an advan- • tage in the play, but the play of the Earlestown backs and goal keeper was splendid, and all attacks of the visitors were repelled. A few minutes before time was called the home forwards had their opponent'a goal at their mercy, but amid disappointing shouts the ball was kicked over the cross-bar, though the player was but a few yards frern the goal. No farther point being registered by either ream the result was declared a draw of two goals each. The E tries- tonians claimed that they had won the match, but that they had been robbed of their victory by the adverse d.cisions of the referee. WARRINGTON (ASSOCIATION) V EVERTOR. - Everton journeyed to Warrington last Sattaday to play the return match. The kick off was announced for ealf-past two, but as the visitors w,re late play was not commenced until three o'clock. The home captain has log won the toss elected to play with a slight wind in his favour, and upon the ball being set in mo:lon by the visitors it was quickly taken possession of by the home forwards, but to no effect as the play for some time was very eveady contested. How- ever, the home team worked well togeqber, showing by far the better play of the twoond began to press their opponents I very closely and their citadel was several times in great I danger. Dillon and Matthews on the left worked well for the home team, and after some good passing took the bill up the wing, whereupon Dillon nicely centered, and the op- portunity was made good use of by Webster, who scored the first goal for the home team, much to the glee of the spec- ' tators, who appeared to take a great interest in the game. The ball was soon set rolling again be' the visitors' centre, I and was taken possession of by the home team, but their at- tempt at scoring was frustrated by Richards, and the visitors, who were not to be denied, got possession, and the centre nicely passing to the left Jackson made a good run, having evaded the backs and with a well-directed shot soon equalized matters. Play was again commenced, and for some time the ball was continually out of play on the left, but the visitors' forwards again got possession and were nearly on the point of scoring, when Davies came to the rescue and cleared the goal in grand style, and sent the bill up the field. After some very even play on both sides, hands was claimed by the home teem in the centre of the field, and upon the ball being entrusted to Royston, who placed it I well, Parker with a good shot succeeded in placing another goal to the credit of the home team. Before play was re- sumed half-time was called, the'score being, Warrington 2, Everton 1. Upon ends being changed both teams were soon at work agar), the visitors being the first to commence operations, whereupon Webster t3ok possession and made a good run, but his attempt at scoring failed. The ball for some considerable time was kept in the visitors' quarters. Now and then a rush would be made only to be again foiled by the home backs, and the forwards still continued to press the visitors, their goal keeper having to handle several times to save his colours. The visitors, however, seemed to rally a little, and by working well together the home fortress was in danger of being taken, the goal keeper being com- pelled to handle. Play still continued to go on, the home team having the beat of it, and from a throw in on the left, Dillon got possession and by a well directed shot (a stinger) sent the ball spinning between the posts, thus adding another goal in favour of the home team. Some little time after play had again been resumed the visitors, with a com- bined rush, appeared to be dangerous, and were on the point of scoring when Scott ( who was at this time off side) suc- ceeded in placing the ball between the home uprights, but on the plea of off side the game was brought to a stand- still, and as the umpires could not agree and time went on the visitors left the field, the time being nearly up and darkness fast approaching, thus leaving the home team victorious by three goals to one. It would be unfair to mention any names in particular, as all the team played well and up to the mark. The goals were scored by Webster, E. Parker, and Dillon. Teams : Warrington—Goal, B. Parker ; backs, Davies (captain) and Royston ; half-backs, E. Parker, Pearson, and Jones ; forwards, Dillon, Matthews, Webster, Siddall, and Allen. Everton—Goal, Hughes; backs, Rich- ards and E. Gunn; half-backs, Pima?, and A. Gunn ; forwards, D. H. Williams, Scott, W. M. Williams, Jackson, and Douglas.
