These teams met on the ground of the latter, on Saturday lar, to play the return match. The first half was very well con- I tested, although the borne team had to touch down twice, I but on changing ends the visitors warmed to their work, I and quickly asserted their superiority, compelling the home I team to act on the defensive nearly the whole of tl.e time. 1, they having to resort to kicking the ball dead and touching , down several times, until at last J. Boardman succeeded in getting a try, which W. Lane converted into a goal. On the call of no side Newton were the victors by one goal and eight minor points to nil. The first match also resulted in a win for Newton. Teams —Newton:: G. Lens (captain) back; S. Rimmer, J. Attall, and J. Boardman' three- quarter-backs ; T. Egan and W. Lane half-backs ; H. Liptrott, W. W. Mee, R. Hitchen, WI Pennington, A. Latimer, T. Egan, sen., T. Braddock, T. Fairclougb, and another, forwards; umpire, G. Fitzgerald. Pagefield : ' T. Blezerd, back ; W. Isherwood, M. Divine' and J. HAWN. I ber, threequarter-backs ; J. Roberts and W. Appleton. half-backs; J. Lowe, F. Wchardeon, J. E. Lowe, W. Pilkington, S. Leitch, R. Thorp, J. Dowling, T. Brether- ton, and G. Tinsley, forwards ; umpire, J. E. Winstan- ley ; referee, Mr. J. Berry. The second teams should have met at Newton, but Pagefield were unable to raise a I team. WARRINGTON V. SALFORD (A TEAM).—These teams rime on Saturday on the ground of the latter There were about 1,600 spectators present. Warrington won the toss, and Gregson started the ball for the borne team, and the visitors 1 failing to return, a scrimmage was formed in neutral ground, where Ashton, Turner, and Povey were seen to great advan- tage. Barnes here made several attempts at goal, but all went wide. Play ranged chiefly in the Salford quarters up to half time, the home team saving twice by touching down. Turner re-started the ball for Warrington and Box- ton returned into neutral ground, when a grand rush by the Salford forwards, headed by Pratt, brought play on to the visitors' line, but Turner, Povev. and Davies were equal to the occasion, and cams through the scrimmage, which , caused the home team to save again. Another deal ball was the only incident until Belshew gained possession and looked like getting over, but was tackled by Williams, and passing to Massey, he made a good attempt to drop a goal, the ball fal ing a little short of the crossbar, a touchdown 11 resulting. Jolley was next seen to advantage, Pratt saving i by kicking the ball dead. Play ranged in Salford quarters up to the call of no side, when the wore was as follows: , Warrington, four touchdowns; Salford, nil. For Warring- I ton Belshaw, Gilbert, and Speakman were best behind, . while in the pack Povey, F. Turner, Ashton, and Davies I shone most. For the home team Timmins, Buxton, Pratt, and Gregson worked hard. Warrington team :—Walsh. full back; Barnes, Massey, Belshaw, threequarter-backe; Gilbert and Speakman, half-backs; Aehton (captain), F. Tarner' Davies, Povey, Frank Turner, Hayes, Jolley, Dillon, and Rigby, forwards. RUNCORN V. FCCLES —The Runcorn first team travelled ' to Eccles on Saturday to play off the return fixture, the home team, after a match of sixty minutes' duration, being ' defeated by one try two touchdowns to three touchdowns. H. Hughes kicked off against the wind, the ball bounding into the home half, where a series of attempts to score were made by Johnson, Wright, and H. Hughes, Johnson being , pushed into touch close to the line. Following the throw out, play ensued in the Runcorn quarter, chiefly by the play of Bury and Vickers. At this juncture Speakman re- lieved ; Johnson gaining more ground, kicked in touch; ! and a subsequent scrimmage, in which the visitors' for- wards strive hard, restaged in Lythgoe being forced to save, H. Wright being close on the ball. Quick play on the part of the Runcorn forwards followed Worthington's drop out. A punt into touch by W. Hughes was the means of a further attack on the tome hue. Andrews, ever ready, was soon over, 'l3-eit on an appeal to the referee, the point was decided against him, owing to some previous infringement from centre. Vickers kicked to Woods, who was equal to the pressure, and nicely cleared past half flag, but the home players again visited the Runcorn quarter, whore Speakman touched down on the goal line, Woods bi- ing soon after forced to save, being the result of a drop at goal by Wig,nall. After changing ends Bury started the ball, to which H Hughes responded. From a loose scrim- mage in centre Clarke got the ball at his feet, and Gattey joining him, the Eccles line was leached, the latter success- fully grounding the ball. Woods was entreated with the place, and bid fair for goal, the ball striking the up- rights. This reverse roused up the home players. and not infrequently did they appear dangerous, Vickers, Bury, and Worthington doing a lot of useful work, but nothing save a.minor point was the result of their endeavours, a good game ending in favour of Runcorn, whose forwards worked hard. The backs played a fair game, Andrews doing a lot of tackling. Teams : —Runcorn—T Woods, back ; W Hughes, T Johnson, and H Speakman, three-quarter backs; H Hughes and H Andrews, halfbacks; W Wright, F Joule, J Lewis, J Gatley, J Barns, J Hofilend,J Clarke, H Wright, and 0 Cliffe, forwards. Eccles—Potter, back; Bury, Wor- thington, and Wignall, three-quarter backs; Vickers and Lythgoe, half backs; Worthington, Johnson Hyde, Crook, Holt, Shrewsbury, Evans, Mercer, and Fletcher, forwards. EARLESTOWN V. CREWE ALEXANDRA.—The meeting of the Eerlestown and Crewe Alexandra clubs at Earlestewn on Saturday afternoon attracted the largest gate to witness a match that ever assembled in connection with the Earles- town club. The excitement occasioned by the contest was intense, and the large concourse of spectators ware rewarded by witnessing one of the best contested games ever played in the neighbourhood. Some five weeks ago the Earlestown representatives were beaten at Crewe by three gears to two, but it was anticipated that when the return match was played at Eartestown the local team would more than turn the tables on their opponents. The Crewe club turned out its strongest eleven, and were accompanied by a large num- ber of their supporters. From the ranks of the home team the only absentee was Ogden, whose place was filled by Murray, a second eleven man. The teams appeared on the field shortly before three o'clock, and the home captain win- ning the toss he decided to play with the ground and wind in his favour. Snelson started the leather for Crewe, and the play immediately became exciting. Both goals were in turn endangered, but the Earlestonians gradually as- sumed the upperband and pressed the Alexinclrians. After about seven minutes' play the home for- wards exhibited some nice passing, and a strong run down the field ended in Murray notching the first goal for Earlestown, amid lend cheers. 1 The question of legalising professionalism in connection with football came before a large attended general meeting of the Football Aesoc;ation, held at the Freemasons' Tavern, London, on Monday night. For the proposals of the Com- mittee in favour of professionalism 113 voted, and 103 I against. As toere was not the necessary two-thirds majority, professionalism still remains illegal. : The news was received in Nottingham on Saturday of the death, in Florida, of Mr. A. W. Cureham' the famous football .layer. Mr. Cursham frequently took part in in- ternational matches, and was at one time perhaps the best forward player in Eugland. The Notts team, of which Mr. Cursham was formerly captain, during their match on Sat- urday with Blackburn Olympic, wore mourning armlets on their jerseys. The principal match in the Lancashire district on Satur- day afternoon was the one played between Bradford and Oldham, which resulted in a draw, the former obtaining 15 minor points to three. Mr. John Bright, writing to Dr. Foster, who has been adopted as a Liberal candidate for Chester, expresses his strong disapproval of the proposed disfranchisement for life of persons who have been " scheduled" by Bribery Commissioners. At the Middlesex Sessions on Wednesday, George Bland was indicted for having been concerned with others in in- tim3dating a number of workmen. The prisoner was found guilty, and sentenced to three months' hard labour in de- fault of paying a fine of £2O. A STATIONMASTER KILLED.—The body of John Welsh, stationmaster at Craige, on the Caledonian Railway, was found dead on the line nett' Portletben, five miles from Aberdeen, on Thursday morning. The deceased had been on a visit to Portletben, and it is supposed that while walk- ing along the line on his way borne he was run down by an express train and killed. ALLEM]) POISONING—The trial of James Day, a farmer, on a charge ef poisoning his aunt, Matilda Hicks, was con- cluded on Thursday at Taunton assizes. The defence was that there was no a-signable motive for the crime, as it had been shown that the prisoner would suffer by the death of Mrs. Hicks. The pry, after deliberating nearly an hour, acquitted the prisoner. Mns. WELDON aoms.—The long-pending case of "Wel- don v. Riviere " was finally disposed of in the Court of Ap- peal on IVedneslay, by M. Riviere paying £2 which Mrs. Weldon demanded, she having paid that sum for netting down her appeal. The defendant's application for a new trial was abandoned. In accordance with a suggestion of the Master of the Rolls, M. Riviere and Mrs. Weldon left the court by doors on opposite sides. &worm POLICE INSPECTOR —A dastardly crime is reported from South Essex. On Tuesday Inspector Sim- mons, of Romford, accompanied by another police officer named Marden, was engaged-watching the movements of three well-known criminals, who according to one account were well-known burglars, while another report states that they were engaged on a poaching enterprise. Early in the evening the officers cfonfronted the men, and when they made off followed them. Two of the gang, upon finding th it the pollee were gaining upon them, turned round and etch fired a pistol, the inspector receiving one of the charges in the lower part of his stomach. Marden con- tinued the chase until he discovered that his inspector was wounded, when he gave up the pursuit, and, having ob- tained assistance, conveyed his wounded comrade to Rom- ford, where medical skill was called into requisition. On Wednesday Inspector Simmons was in a dangerous condi- tion, and no hopes are held out of his recovery. The inspec• tor has made a deposition in which he states that be was tcquainted with one of the men who attacked him, and that his name is David Dodge. ' None of the men have been arrested. div.head: TUB COST OF LUNATICS.
div.p: TUB COST OF LUNATICS.

I Mr. DARBYSHIRE said that on looking over the accounts !he saw that they load nearly 5.00 to pay at that meeting for the maintenance of lunatics. He did not know whether or not that was an Increase on previous payments, hut if it was he wished that something could be done to stop it. It was a very heavy sum to pay, and people outside wondered where all the money went to. The lunatic asylums formed , one of the heaviest sources of the payments of that Union. —The Citatamati said that at a later stage the clerk would give them a statement so that they might have the matter I properly discussed.—Mr. HeaursoN said the increase in payments with regard to lunatics seemed to be universal.— Mr. BL&CIEHIMIST remarked that one of the causes of in- creased payments was that imbeciles who were formerly kept at the Workhouse, were now sent to the asylurn.—The subject then dropped.

-SC HOOL FEES COHMITTEFL This committee report that it had dealt with 143 appli- cations for school fees, 31 of which were new ones and 112 eld.—Mr. BLACKAUEST, who moved the adoption of the committee's minutes, said he was sorry to say that these ap- plications were on the increase.—Mr. JOLLEY, in sec3gding, remarked that the increase would probably be only a matter of a few weeks during the winter season.—The minutes were adopted.

div.p: AN ENTERTAINUENT.

The Workhouse Master reported that members of the Bank Quay Working Men's Mission had given an entertain- ment to the inmates, which had been much enjoyed.—The Chairman of the Board (Mr. Greening), presided.—Mr. APPLETON : Was it a teetotal aff dr, Mr. Chairman ?—The CHAIRMAN : They were members of a teetotal society that were there. I had very great pleasure in presiding, and shall have great pleasure in presiding again if required. (Bear, hear.)

div.head: TRADESMEN'S ACCOUNTS.
div.p: TRADESMEN'S ACCOUNTS.

The CHArrem 4N mentioned that the auditor had recently been auditing the Caion accounts. Be had sent for him (the chairman) with respect to two surcharges, one of £5 13s. and Ito other cf 15s 8.1, and after a considerable con- versation he agreed to withdraw the surcharges. The reason of the surcharges was—and he (the chairman) wished them all to know it—that part of an account sent in was overdue, and there was not only that one but several. Tne auditor pointed it out as an instance of the Way trades- men had of not sending in their accounts at the proper time, be consequently having to disallow them. After some explanation the auditor said that if he (the chairman) and Mr. Sutton would take notice that in the future the accounts were either properly sentin or struck out altogether he would not surcharge them on that occasion. He (the chairman) promised that as far as be was concerned such a thing should not happen again, aud the Clerk ronised the same. If in the future tradesmen did not send in their ac- counts in proper time they would be the losers themselves. There was an account from Mr. Hall, and they had had to ask the Local Government Board to allow them to pay it, because of its not being rent in at the proper time. The Local Government Bed had struck part of it out and eaid they might pay the remainder, therefore Mr. Hall would be the loser of the amount struck out.—Mr: CALDWELL thought that would be an injustice.—The CHAIRMAN said he did not see any injustice in the matter. If people would not send in their accounts when they knew they ought to be sent in they must take the loss. He had made his re- marks in order that members of the Board and the public might know that the delay in sending in accounts must be put an end to.—Mr. CALDWELL said there was no doubt that the orders of the Local Government Board must be at- tended to, but he thought it would be bard if anyone was to lose because their account had not been sent in time, and he suggested that they be paid if the Board could do it legally. He also suggested that a notice should be put on the written order sent to tradesmen stating when the ac• count had to be sent in.—The CLERK mentioned that it was stated on the order that al soon as it was executed the account was to be sent in. The object, he said, of the ac- counts being sent in in proper time was that the expendi- tore during any particular period should appear in the list of expenditure for that period.—Mr. DARBYSIIIRE thought that ties delay in sending in the accounts aroze more from carelessness than anything else, and he hoped the Board would assist the chiirm an to carry out his promise to the auditor and never pay any account sent in late, leaving the tradesmen to get the money themselves from the Local Government Board.—The Crummeze said that in the future he would sign no more cheqcus to pay accounta not sent in at the proper time.—The subject then dropped. THE DISPUTE WITH NEWTON COMMISSIONERS.

The CLERK said, with reference to the question of the Harris family, that he had written to Mr. Brierley to say that all the circumstances of this case had been put before the Local Government Board by the Guardians who would be advised by the Local Government Board. He (the clerk) had received the following letter, dated Bth January, from Mr J. E. Woreley, law clerk to the Newton Commis- sioners, viz —"I: am instructed by the Newton Commis- sioners to apply to the Warrington Guardians for payment of the expenses incurred by the Commissioners in respect of the maintenance and nursing at the Warrington Hospital of George Harris's family, the said George Harris being a lodger at Newton and a person without the means of ob- taining for his family (who were suffering from fever) the medical attendance, nursing, and maintenance requisite for them. I am informed that the Gaurdians at Newton have had the case before them and made an order, that Mr. Brier- ley has afterwards applied to you for the money, and that he and I r. Watkins have had an interview with you upon the subject, and that the money remains unpaid • I am now instructed to say that in the event of the account not being paid by Tuesday next the Commissioners will COM- mence proceedings against the Guardians for its recovery. With a view of avoiding litigation in the matter, I would direct your attention to the very decisive opinion given in these cases by the Local Government Board in their letter to me on the 13th April, 1881, a copy of which you have, and to your letter to me of the 7th March, in the same year, undertaking on behalf of the Guardians to pay in these cases in the future if the Catnmissioners subscribed to the Fever Hospital."—Mr. HARRISON: Have the Newton Commissioners paid that money to the Warrington authori- tiesl—The CLERK: I don't know.—Mr HARRISON: How CIA they sue us if they have not paid it P—The CHAIRMAN: I suppose they will have paid it.—The CLERK said that to this letter he replied as follows: Dear Sir,— Mr. Brierley has already been told that all the papers are before the Local Government Board, who will doubtless advise the Guardians. There can be no possible reason for, and no poesible alvantage from, hurried litigation. Your references to an "undertaking" by me evidences the mis- understanding existing between the Commissioners and the Guardians, and between their respective officers All through and all round I have tried to make clear the differ- ence between isolation of infectious persons and their relief if relief is necessary; It is by confunding the two things, instead of viewing them to be separate and distinct, confu- sion and perplexity result. I feel sure, looking alone at what has happened in connection with the case of Harris's family, you must have had misgivings as to the Claim you ; make—if it is not so, if you seriously mean that the Com- missioners can hold the Guardians liable in such circum- stances RS these wre assumed to be, prior to your know- I ledge the Relief Committee having made an order, I will I advise the Guardians to test their liability in a court of law. If, as I judge, you have learned, as no doubt you , have, what at an interview with Dr. Watkins and Mr. Brierley I did not know that the Relief Committee made an , order, and that whereas without such an order success did not seem clear, with it the grouad is clear, then I ask you ' to await the result of the action of the Board of Guardians upon that order, which was made on my advice, although not in the ferns I would have recommended. No purpose can be served by litigation upon that particular order, your general contention, if you swiously advice it to the Com- missioners, seems to me to be wholly intenable, and I have the most perfect confidence in no such liability attaching to a Board of Guardians. However, by all means defer the litigation you are properly desirous to avoid until Ton hear from the Guardians definitely. My letter, of course, ' ia without prejuilice."—On the 13th Jan., Mr Worslev wrote to the clerk, in reply to the above letter, as follows: ft was nearly six o'clock before your letter was delivered last night, and it did not come to my hands until this morning, or it would have been answered before Oil. My instructions were to commence proceedings to-day, and had I not received your letter I should have done so. As it is I will put off until three o'clock to-morrow, beyond that time I cannot go, nor do I think after most carefully read- ing your letter that there is anything to be gained by any delay. The facts are perfectly clear and perfectly well- known to both of us. Your medical officer took the case, and your relieving committee made an order. The opinion of the Local Government Board was taken on a former oc- casion, and governs this case. Delays with a six months' statutory limitation are extremely dangerous." To this the Clerk again replied as follows :—" No advantage will be taken by the Guardians of any statute of limitation. You need not therefore have no cause for hurry on that ground. Nothing Can be more deplorable than the great waste of pub- lic money in this canntry upon litigation. The law and the facts are in this case disputed •, if the Newton Com- missioners are in the right it requires no litigation to make them so—the Guardians, as must be clear to you, are acting in the matter in a way that ought to meet your approval. If the Commissioners are determined to rush into law, of course I cannot help it. -My letter is without prejudice." The Local Government Board, the Clerk continued, to whom the matter had been referred, wrote to him on the 15th to say that they had communicated with the Newton Commissioners on the subject. As the matter was under the consideration of the law advisers of the Local Govern- ment Board, counsel of very high standing and familiar both with the law and its practice, he (the clerk) thought it was a lamentable thing that the Commissioners could not wait till they bad received the opinion of the Local Go- vernment Board. (Hear, bear). He had, however, been served with a county cotert summons, the claim being for £32 43. That was certainly adopting the court in which the case could be easiest fought out if , it was to be fought out, but at the seine time ' be would point out that it was really a case in which I ratepayers of Newton were fighting against ratepayers of Newton. If the Newton Commissioners won the case the ratepayers of Newton would have to pay is for every penny they would gain by the tact that they would have to con-

tribute for the Warrington costs. It seemed injudicious even if they were right, that they should go into coat with this case. (Hear, hear.) However, heasked for the in- structions of the Board as to whether It was a case in which a solicitor should appear, and instruct counsel. Mr. APPLETON asked if there had not been an arrangement made two or three years ago, between that Board and the Newton Commissioners, as to paying for those sort of cases. —The CLERK said the position had been entirely misunder- stood. What he had said all through was that as far as the isolation of infectious cases was concerned, it was for the advantage of the inhabitants of the district and it was the duty of the Sanitary Authority to provide it. He went further and said that if an application was made to a Board of Guardians that a man wee not in a position. because of sickness, to procure the comforts of family nursing and maintenance and 80 on. that man became a pauper. It was then the duty of the Board of Guardians to provide for him, not because it was are infectious case, it did not matter what the sickness or where in the Union the MAR lived. They would give relief just the same as if the man bail been at the house, and it was any other disease than infections dis- ease. He (the clerk) also pointed out that the Newton Commissioners bad nothing to do with the order for relief. , The order had been given in just the same way as any other order for relief, and they were not responsible to the Newton Commissioners—Mr. BLACERMIST said that al- though it was never desirable to enter into litigation, it was beet to let this case Us fought out in the County Court, so that they might know in future who was reeponsible for similar cases.—Mr. APPLETON thought the Guardians were really not liable for that case, and he was of the same opinion as the clerk that where a penny would be rained by the ratepayers of Newton, a shilling would be lost by the liti- gation. If they had to defend ihemselves he would suggest that Mr. Jeans be the solicitor entrusted with the CUL —Mr. JOLLEY supported the proposal. He said Mr. Jeans had just told him that he would conduct thecae voluntarily and this he thought showed that Mr. Jeans had the interests of the Guardians at heart. (Hear, hear.) He (Mr. Jolley) was of opinion that the Newton Commissioners had behaved in a very discourteous manner, and concluded by moving that Mr. Jeans be instructed to take all the necessary means to defend the Guardians.—Mr. CaLrawiret, suggested that they should try some peaceful means of settling the diapute and not knock their heads together in the County Court. At the same time, he thought that Mr. Jeans deserved a medal not merely of gold but of diamonds because be was the &rat lawyer who in his (Mr. ualitwell's) experience had ever volunteered to take a case without pay.—Mr. DARBYSTURg thought their clerk was quite able to defend the case himself without their engaging counsel.—Mr. JEANS emit that in this case he was quite sure they had the law on their side.— After some further discussion Mr. liaanisoti said he did not tbiok they ought to accept Mr. Jeans' generous offer, but engage him in the usual way. (Hear, hear )—The resolution that Mr. Jeans be instructed to take the necessary means to defend in the pending action was put and carried ulanimously, after which the subject dropped.
A VACANCY. It was resolved to advertise for a person to fill the pules of Miss Mackey, schoolmistress at the Workhouse, who has resigned.
Titis concluded the business of public interest.

REDISTRIBUTION. SOITTH-WEST LANCASHIRE. The official scheme for the partition of South-West , Lancashire is as follows :—The seven electoral areas it is proposed to name the Southport, Ormskirk, Bootle, Widnes, Newton, Rice, and Leigh divisions respectively. The Southport division (population 57,643) includes the parishes of Great and Little Crosby, Thornton, and Ince Blundell, the petty sessional division of Southport, the municipal borough of Southport. The Ormskirk division (population 54,9)7), com- prises the parishes of Knowsley, Croxteth P.rk, Up. holland, Presoet, Kirkby, Aintree, Netherton, Sef - ton, Litherland, Orrell, and Ford, and Lunt, and the petty sessional division of Ormskirk The Bootle division (population 48491), includes the parishes of Bootle•cum-Linaker, Walton-on-the Hill, Fazakerley, Wavertree, Chitdwall, and parts of West Derby; and Toxteth Park outside the city, and the city of Liverpool. The Widnes division (population 53 )51), com- prises the parishes of Uareton, Allerton, Mitch Woll• ton, Little Woolton, Halewood, Speke, and Hale. and the petty sessional division of Prescott, except the parishes of Prescot, Rainhill, Knoveeley, and Croxteth Park. The Newton division (population 51.201), includes the Parishes of Culcheth, Ashton-ineMekerlielcl, and Rainhill, the petty sessional divisions of St. Helens I and Warrington, and part of the municipal borough of Warrington. The Ince division (population 53 851), comprises the parishes of Haigh, Ince in-Alakeritield, Pember- ton, Hindley, Orrell, Winstanley, Billenge Chapel End, and Billenge Higher End, and the municipel borough of Wigan. The Leigh division (population 52,187), includes the parishes of Atherton, Tyldeeley -with-Shakerley, Astley, Pennington, and West Leigh, Bedferd, Abram, Kenyon, and Lowton. The Hon. T. H. W. Pelham will open an inquiry in Liverpool on the 24th inst. It is estimated that the totel number of voters will be between 70e000 and 80,000. Soon"- EAST Lswessuran.—The Boundary Commis- sion sat on Saturday at Whitehall and agreed upon the following provisional scheme for this division of the electoral area of South East Leneashire : The Eccles Division, population 61 959, to consist of Worsley, Clifton, Pendlebury, Barton•upon•lrwell, Flizton, and Urmston. The Stretferd Division, population 51,047, to consist of the parishes of Strtt. ford, Chorlton-cum-Hardy, Withington, Di.ishury, Moss Side, Rusholme, Bradford, Harpurhey, Newton, Burnage, Heaton Norris (pert of), Levenshulatte, and the municipal boroughs of Salford and Stockport (part of), and the city of Manchester. Noarn•Esse Lin &snras.— The inquiry necessary to determine the best mode of dividing North-East Lancashire in accordance with the requirements of the Redistribution Bill, was held on ‘Veduesday at Preston, before the Hon. T. H. W. Pelham, one of the Boundary Commissioners. Sir U. Kay-Shuttleworth, speaking on behalf of both political parties in the Accrington, Rossendale, and Clitheroe divisions, submitted a scheme dif- fering in some of its details from that propoun- ded by the Commissioners. By this scheme the Clitheroe division is made to include a larger portion of the Calder Valley, which it is desired should be preserved intact if possible. The re- presentatives of Darwen opposed this scheme, and also objected to the large rural population which, under the plan of the Commissioners, is to be included in that division. During the inquiry numerous gentlemen expressed their opinion that the scheme which was published some time ago, and which is known as th.e "East Lancashire Scheme," was better than any which has since been suggested. The Commissioner, however, hold out no hope that it would be adopted by hitnself and his colleagues. Notelet LLNCA.IIIIIE.—The Hon. T. H. W. Pelham one of the Boundary Commissioners, sat for upwards of four hours on Tuesday at Lancaster listening to modifications suggested in the scheme which the Com- missioners have proposed for,diving North Lancashire into four electoral districts. Mr. John Fell, speaking on behalf of a committee representing b3th political peteies in North Lancashire, strongly opposed the scheme of the Commissioners, and recommended that the boundaries of the hundreds should be adopted for the proposed divisions, North Leasdale being consti- tuted a separate Parliamentary area. A number of gentlemen from Balckpool and other places expressed approval of the plan drawn up by the Commissioners, but it was freely criticised by most of those who at- tended the inquiry in an official or representative capacity. Mr. L. Revestorne, the chairman of the Conservative Association of North Lancashire, acting on a suggestion frem the Commissibner, submitted an alternative scheme, to which, he said, they desired consideration should be given by the Boundary Com- missioners if it was found impossible to take the hundreds as furnishing the best dividing lines. Sonic remarks which Mr. Pelham let fall during the inqniry seemed to indicate that he will recommend his brother Commissioners to modify their scheme to a greater or less extent in certain of the directions suggested yes- terday. YOBILSIIME.—The six electoral areas of the eastern division of the West Riding, it is suggested shall be named the Ripon, the Otley. the Hazlowooil, the Os- golderose, the Padsey, and the Cleckheaton divisions respectively. The eight electoral areas of the southern division of the West Riding, it is proposed to name the Morley, Normanton, Colne Valley, Peaistoue, Barnsley, Ecclesfield, Rothetham, and Doncaster divi- sloes respectively. LONDON.—The Boundary Commission began work in London on Saturday, and dispesed of four consti- tuencies. Kensington was split into two divisions. The Northern part includes a population of 82,517 while in the South division there is a population of 80,864. In Marylebone the dividing line runs north and south. The east division has a population of 71,039, and the west divisiop a population of 88,874. On Monday inquiries were held at St. Pancras and Islington to hear objections to the proposed constitu- tion of the new constituencies. In neither case was the inquiry long.

GOLBORNE. Smut SERVICES.—During the week special rev al services have been goir,g on at the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Bildee-street, under the supervision of the Rev. T. Vaughan, resident minister. liiiN-ETEILFRB Drarnmann.—At an early hour on Thurs- day morning a daring attempt at hen-stealing was frustrated by the police on duty near the Co-operati7e Stores, Heath- ereet. The officers heard the fowls making a noise, and were informed by a Mn. Seddon that there WU some one In the yard. The police proceeded thither, whereupon the would.be robbers decamped. The hen-cote had been broken into, but no fowls were missed. TEA PARTY AND ENTERTAINMENT.—The members of M. Woolacott's young men's Bible class arranged a tea party for Saturday evening and made provision for the admiesion of their friends. Mr. Brewis's scl•ools were kindly lent for the occasion, and at the appointed hour about 251 persons Were present. The class, which wa9 ettrted twelve months ago and which meets every Sunday a.fternoon, now consists of 00 young men. A short interval followed an excellent tea, and then an interesting meeting was comm ncid, Mr. Arnott being elected to preeide.—The Chairman, after referring tie the absence of the Rector through illness, is;,oke of the pro- gress Sr. Thomas's Senior Bible Class had made under the zealous efforts of Mr. Woolacott. Such a class, be said, was sure to exert an influence for go nd in the neighbourhood. Grimke next gave a magic lantern entertainment a a high class order. The stories illustrated were told in a man- ner calculated both to please and instruct young and old. The remainder of the entertainment includ Mg pianoforte Solon, singing, reciting, dte., appeared to be much appreciated. —A vote of thanks to all concerned w.s pa-sed with much cordiality.

DU SAD ICE FATALITY AT CrOLBORNE. Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, hell an inquest at the Anget Hotel, Edge-green, on Saturday, touching the death of James Hnsworth, aged 17. who was drowned %%Mist skating on a pond within a few yards from his father's house, on the previous Wednesday.— From the evidedce of tbe mother and a brother, it appeared that the youth, who, had not been home to dinner for many months previously. get up from the dinner table and went immediately to the pond to skate. When he was in the water a long prop and a clothes line were thrown to him, but deceased appeared to take no notice of them. They did all they could to save him. The body was recovered in about half-an-hour.—The Coroner paid it was one of those ice accidents which un- fortunately had been very frequent of late. He had just come from a similar inquiry at Sutton. Boys and men were too venturesome ; they went on the ice before it would hold, and the consequence was there was no getting them out again. In the present case a Police-Officer (Police-con- stable Corser, of Golborne), saw the lad sink, but as he arrived too late he (the coroner) did not thick it necessary to take his additional evidence.—rne Foreman : There was no one to blante.—A verdict of accidental death was returned. At the suggestion of the jury the coroner drew up a presentment to the effect that as there were in that district several pits of deep water in close and dangerous proximity to the highways in an entirely unfenced condi- tion, which were dangerous to paesengers sod children, the jury urged the local authorities to take immediate action to have the same filled up or fenced if. The coroner added that if any further accident happened before that order was attended to, someone would likely have a warm shop of it. Deceased's funeral took place on Saturday afternoon, at St. Thomas's Ce urct , and was ;witnessed by a large number of fellow teachers acd scholars. A brother of deceased was killed at a neighbouring colliery some few years ago.

- - - SCHOOL BOARD.—The monthly meeting of the Prescot School Board could not be held on Monday evening, owing to the absence of a quorum. The only members present were Messrs. C. Speneely and 1. P Hewitt. The quarterly report of Inspector 11.)ylis stated that 35 children hak reached the age cf five years, and were attending the fol- lowing schools :—Clicirob 12, Board 8, Yew Tree 9, and private 6. Eight families had left the town, whose ID children attended schools :—Board 16, Yew '1 ree 2, and Church 2. One family had come to reside in tLe town, whose two children were attending the Board schools. During the holidays five stoves had been supplied to the schools, and they were working rails actorily. PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIA.NB.—The fortnightly meet- ing was held on Thursday, at the Wh;e!en Workhouee. Mr. J. T. Hall presided The ?nester reported that there were 471 inmates this week, against 460 in the corresponding period of last year A letter was read from Mr Wallace Revill, lessee of the Theatre Royal, St. Helens, inviting the juvenile inmates to a performance of .his pantomime, " The Babes in the Wood." The clerk was instructed to acknow- ledge the kind offer, and to inform Mr. Revill that the children were at present in the Klikdale Schools, so . that they would not he able to attend. Another letter was read from Mr. Henry Suinner, architect.. Liverpool, enclosing drawings and spcifications for new infirmary at the workhouse, and asking the Guardians to obtain the sanction of the Local Government Board to the same. The matter was referred to the Building Committee. —Mr. G. Hatlehurst, district auditor, intimated by letter that on Monday, February 9, be would attend at the work- house for the purpose of audirng the union accounts for the balf•year ending December 20, 1881.

They were advised that if the proposed sewage depots were carried out on the site shown on the plan the water supply of St. Helens would be, if not absolutely polluted and rendered useless, seriously affected. Mr. 1.). F. M. Gaskin, C.E., F.G.S , said\ he was the St - Helens borough water engineer. If the ProPosal sewage depots were made on the sites shown on the plan the water supply of St. Helens was likely to be seriously affected. The Ecclesten Hill well was 870 yards distant and the Whie'‘on well was about a mile and a quarter distant. These wells were the chief source of water supply for the borough of St. Helens. The bottom of the Eccleston Hill well was 50 or 60 feet below the level of the proposed depo' t at Ec- cleston ; and the bore-hole was 178 feet lower. div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, JANUARY 24, 1885.

SIR STAFFORD NORTHCOTE and Mr. JOHN BRIGHT have both been engaged during the past week in addressing the new electorate —the former by means of a speech, and the latter by the medium of a letter. Both men are eminent as politicians—Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE as the leader of the Conservative party in the House of Commons, and Mr. BRIGHT as the Tribune of the People in and out of Parliament. Both start from the same point—the great fact of the passing of a mea- sure of reform which admits Two Millions of men within the pale of the Constitution ; both are looking forward ; and it is therefore of special interest to note what each has to say to those who will shortly be called upon, and for,the first time, to send representatives to St. Stephen's. To begin with the Devon- shire baronet, it is'a matter of course that what he has to say should be urged in the gentlest tones. He is "the mildest mannered man that ever scuttled ship or cut a throat." If a Professor of Moderation were required for any of our Universities, and if Sir STAF- FORD NORTHCOTE were among the competi- tors, it cannot be doubted that be would by common consent be elected to the chair. It is needless to confess that we like him in that he lets his "moderation be known unto all men"; but at the same time when it becomes a matter of leading us somewhere it is necessary to ask—Where are you going? and what are you going to do? To these questions Sir STAFFORD has no answer—none at any rate that the n:mly-enfranchised will regard as satisfactory. He admits that the new voters will have to elect members "to deal with questions bearing upon the interests of labour ; but he tails to make it clear what part or lot the Conservative party will have in legislating in "the interests of labour." It is true there is the usual talk about doing all that is possible to "increase and strengthen the British Empire ;" but wind of this kind will not fill the sails of those who look to the franchise as a means of improving their condition in life; the labourer asks for Bread and the Conservative leader has nothing better to offer than the Stone at which the half starved wretch has been gnawing since he came into the world. "Their duty towards those men," he said, "was to instruct them as to the greatness of the responsibility which they undertake, and the question of the interests with which they would have to deal, and the spirit in which they ought to undertake them." Let all this be granted; but what then? Is there noth- ing more? Have "those men" no interests in the soil they cultivate beyond the miser- able pittance which they at present obtain, and the propect of terminating existence at the poor-house? Alas! when it comes to a vital issue the Oracle is dumb ; not a word of promise tothrowat a dog; but words of warn- ing are plentiful as blackberries. " What he was afraid of," he added, "was that the matter would not be allowed to arrange itself, and that an opportunity might be taken of ex- citing those people to believe that they had great wrongs to be redressed, great aims to accomplish, and that they had it before them

now to put themselves on an equality with those better off than themselves." This, at any rate, is a bit of good old-fashioned Tory- ism, and we thank Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTZ for his candour. It is a pity he didn't " d.rop into verse ;" he might have expressed hinl- self more pithily, and greatly embellished his speech, by saying— Bless the Squire ana his relations And keep as in our proper stations. "Great wrongs to be redressed, great aims to accomplish," that is all nonsense in the

_ Opinion of Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE. Let us turn now to Mr BRIGHT. He goes back, as he usually does, to history for proof of his statements that the Liberal party has; always been in favour, as it is to-day, showering blessings upon the people, and of - extending their power. They are reminded of the fact that they owe it to the Liberal ' party that they possess the ballot which- makes the vote of the poor as safe as that of' the rich; and that bread to-day is about half the price at what the Corn-Laws intended it to', be when the home harvest happened to be bad. "Some of the Tories, says 111 r.: - BRIGHT, "are now proposing to restore the'4 law, and again to make the labourers' bread" dearer, so that farmers may be able to paf rents which they say are too high unless the- law is put in force to raise the market price - of wheat and the baker's price of bread! ' Iri other words, if the ,Tories come into power, and certain of them haye their way, ever? working-man in the Kingdom will be called upon to pay a higher price for the bread he e eats in order that aristocratic land-owners ' may exact higher rents than the farmer under, normal conditions can afford to pay. BRIGHT refers refers also to the fact that, thanks 0% Liberal legislation, sugar can be had at one: ' third the price which it reached in the days' of Protection, while tea can be purchased less than the amount of the tax which for' merly rested upon it. He points, too, to the cheap Press and cheap schools as boons 14)4 which Liberals pride themselves, and then he, has a word as to the future. "The lana. laws," he says, "will be reformed and much, of them will be reformed out of existence:* There is clearly something wrong when thickly populated country like England—onef' too, with a population always steadily increaV ing—fewer people are being employed o.' that source of all wealth—the land. Agrictuf tural labourers know to their sorrow that the cause is not in the high wages they obtaii.i. and farmers know that they pay in maiii cases so much for rent that they cannot affort. to pay more for labour; The land-owner ,if appealed to, would doubtless tay en , the land ought to yield more th• he gets from it. and he would, in sonic' cases, be right. What, then, is wanted Free trade, we would answer, in land as 0' other commodities. At the present tinleL under our barbarous code of laws, the bul: of the land of this country is so tied up in ot,l` way or another that it cannot reada be brought into the market. There are Intl lions of acres requiring to be drained, 01,1 there are men willing for a fair sum to work hard so that the barren earth may beconl9, fruitful; but, often enough the lordly ovine' of broad acres has no more than a life 10' terest in his estate. He has no spare cash te employ in draining, and fencing, and tilling!. and, if he had, would he not be a fool, 11: would say, to bury it in the earth when the chances were that some distant relatioo... would reap the harvest. And thus-the gaiil? goes on—the land starving for want of car tal expending upon it, and men starving for want of work to do. But we can make changw, in this ; "the whole system of land la/ must be broken down "; we must get rid entail and primogeniture; set free the fore': which to tend to the sub-division of land, aril if need be, insist that human beings shalt have a claim to it prior to that of deer, an grouse, and other game. The Game La.„Lr" will, too, as Mr. BRIGHT states, come revision; so that there will be less teroPn• tion to become poachers, and the {aria' will have a better chance of reaping where he sows. There is, therefore, plenty ,rc/` do; there are "wrongs to be redressed.; and "great aims to accomplish " wh'f ever Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE may 53,1 and the new elector will, we trust ha;o.- the sense to see that the best use he make of his vote is give it to the Libe' party. aci'

INSPECTION OF POLICE AT WIDNES.—YeStOTday after- noon, Captain C. V. Ibbertsen, assistent Chief Constable for Laacashire, inspected the constables of the Prescot Division at Widnes. There were on Parade Superintendent Barker, Inspectors Wood, Peters, and Mayo, and 75 sergeants and constables. The Inspector carefully examined the, clothing and appointments of the officers, and the books in the office, and expressed himself well pleased with all the arrangements. FOUNDERING OF A RUNCORN BOUND VESSEL.— The steamer Clifton, of West Hartlepool, arrived at Dover on Tuesday, and landed the crew of the, brigantine Colla, which she had picked up on the previous day in a boat drifting about in the Channel. The crew were taken to the Dover National Sailors' Home, and late in the day were for- warded to London. The master states that they were bound from Poole to Runcorn, with pipeclay, when their vessel 'prang a leak, and foundered on Saturday last. LECTURE ON OLIVER CROMWELL AT WIDNES. To a large audience at the United Methodist Free Church, Oak- land-street, Widnes, on Monday evening, the Rev. W. Vause delivered a lecture on "Oliver Cromwell, the Uncrowned King of Eogland." in an eloquent manner the rev, gentle- man sketched the principal events in the life of the great commoner—his success on the field of battle, his triumph In diplomacy, and the beneficient results of his wise control of the nation's affairs as Lord protector. Mr. J. R. Hudson presided. FORCIBLY EJECTED AT WESTON.—Edward Lowe, a mid- dle aged man, was brought before the Runcorn magistrates on Monday, charged with being quarrelsome and disorderly on the premises of Arthur Percival, Prospect Inn, Weston, and refusing to leave when requested. On the evening of the fish inst the defendant went to the I?%r the inn, but the landlord said he had had sufficient liquor, and declined to serve him. The defendant then became very noisy, used id language, drank another man's beer, wanted to fight, and altogether misconducted himself. As he refused to leave at the request of the landlord, a constable ejected him. A fine of lOs and costs was imposed. FRODSTIAN PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE. ARTISTIC WINDOWS FOR SANKEY BE.IDGES WBSLIWAN CHAPEL.—The Gioceinati Commercial ,Gazette says.:— "There was placed on exhibition at the Robert Mitchell Furniture Companfe yesterday several beautiful windows in stained glass of much artistic merit. They are after designs by Mr. John R. Gandy, and the work has been carried out by the house under his personal direction. -Special interest attaches to one of theca windows, which is to be sent to England, an offering frotn Mr. Gandy and his brothers to Si little Wesleyan Mi4eion Chapel, Sankey-Bridges near War- rington. This window, which is purely an example of Art in workmanship and material, is some twelve feet and a half by ten, very rich in colour, and beautifully harmonious in treatment. In the centre, against a circle of amber-tinted tongues of flame, playing upon a rich dark green back- groand, is a cross of the crucifixion in pale onyx, and spots the cross-piece is suspended the crown of thorns. Upon a broad, pale blue scroll, which Grosses in graceful undulation the ceatre of the space, are the words • God forbid that I should glory save in the cross of Christ,' the figure of the cross taking the place of the word. The result shows fine artistic effect, secured by the simplest means. About the centre cross and legend are arched bands of amber light, richly fussed, and others in which rondels of vivid crimson are introduced with brilliant results. The whole is ae satie- rectory from 59 artietic view as from that of sentiment,

RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—EarIy on Tuesday morning a goods train broke down between Blackburn and Wilpshire, on the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway, and blocked one line for several hours. On the Midland Railwav, near Mel. ton Mowbray, an express train ran into a hiy cart which had failed to clear a level crossing in time, and smaehed it to pieces. The train was but little damaged.

THE DE ACCIDENT.—At an adjourned irquiry on Wed. I nesdav respecting the drowning of Mr. and Mrs. 'Jackson, of Queen's Ferry, and their infant child, by the sinking of a ferry-boat in the Dee, it appeared that the boat was a small one, in temporary use by the River Dee Company, and altogether unfit to carry more than four or five pel sans. When the accident occurred there were twelve persons on board, and the boat, which leaked badly, filled and went down. Captain Davies was now declared criminally respon- sible, and a verdict of manslaughter returned against him. The bodies of Mr. and Mrs. Jackson have not yet been v- covered.

The death is announced of Mr. Mora L-onnel y, formerly member for Meath, and SeColla son of Liberator. the The Bishop of Liverpool (Dr. Ryle)on Wed nest7ay con- secrated the new Church of St. Agnes, LiverpJol, et: cted by Mr. H. D. liorsfall. Two boys were drowned in a lake near Monagli in on Alm- ' day. One fell through the broken ice and the otlier went to his rescue, with the result stated. IMr. Pickard, the well-known miners' agent, has been ad. opted by the Yorkshire Miners' Association as a labour cin- ' didate for one of the seats allotted to the West Ridieg. A telegram from Boyle, county Roscommon, states that while three young men, two of whom were LI-others, were skiting on Fin Lough, the ice gave waY, and all three were drowned. On Tuesday five of the convicts at Dartmoor were seri- ously injured by ad explosion, caused by the in -n who were engaged in blasting granite accidently striking an old un- exploded hole charged with dynamite. THE WOOLWICH MURDER.— At Woolwich, On Wednesday, Frederick Marshall was charged on remand with the murder of Laura iVilson by stab Ling her at Woolwich cn the 22nd, ult. The accused, who rfserved his defence, was c muait- ted for trial on the capi' a charge.

PRINCE ALBERT Vicron.—The Mayor of Warrington has received from Prince Albert Victor of Wales the fol- lowing acknowledgement of the loyal and dutiful address forwarded to His Royal Highness on the occasion of attain- ing his majority:—" Sandringham, Norfolk, Jan. 13, 1885. To the Mayor, Alde.men, and Burgesses of the Barough of Warrington. Mr. Mayor and Cientlemen,—l cordially thank you for the cmgratulations you offer me on the occasion of my birthday. Your loyal expressions concerning the Queen and the Prince and Princess of Wales I heartily reciprocate. Whatever the future may have in store, I heartily pray that it may co ulnae to the bust interests of the people of these realms,—Albert Victor."

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SLTURDAY.—Before Aldermen Burgess and Chandley. & COMBA.TITE FF.MILF.—A young woman, named Mary Flannery, a fustian cutter, was charged on a warrant with fighting in Winwick-street, on the 26th December.—The police gave the defendant a bad character, andzhe was bound over to keep the peace for six months, herself in £5, and one surety in £5, or in default 14 days' imprison-

ment. Frutons Druvrero —Thomas Lee, a hawker, was charged with having furiously driven a pony along Sankey-street and Buttermerket-street, on the 10th June.—Tbe Bench said they were determined to put a stem to this furious driv- ing in Warrington, and fined defendant lOs and costs, or one month's imprisonment. DROKFNNESS.—James Newton, who lives at Martins- craft, was fined 53 and costs for having been drunk in Buttermarket-street, on the 6,h inst. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Heals( n), in the chair, and Mr. John Fairelough. MISCELLANEOUS.—Tte following were fined for drunken- ness : John Hewitt, in Bridge-street, 55 and costs; Patrick Hanlan in 7:M(11,e-street, Si-and costs; Mary knockton. in 11m-dock-street, 5a and costs ; Bodelia Knockton, in !Putter- market-street, 103 and costs —Winifred Flanigan, charged with sleeping out on ;Sunday morning, was dismissed with a caution.—William Brown and Thomas Lyons were charged with committing a breach of the peace on the 10th inst. by fighting in the Market Flaci. Lyons, who appeared to have been the least to blame, was only ordered to pay costs, and B-own was bound over to keep the peace for six months and ordered to pay costs. SCHOOL Arrnematece.—Mr. G. Riley, school attendance officer, prosecuted in the following cases :—Joseph Allwood, wiredrawer, Friars' Green, fined lOs; in the case of Cather- ine Silcock, whose son was a confirmed truant, the Bench adjourned th 6 summons for a fortnight, upon the under- standing that if the boy did not go to school he would be sent to the training ahip " Clio ;" Pat Hanlon, hawker, Old Gardens, fined sa; Jahn Graham, tanner, Winveick-street, fined 10s in respect of two casts; Thomas Duff, labourer, Watkin-street. fined lOs for two cases; James Gleave, forge- man, Lytbgoea-lane, fined ss; William Blanchard, g,lass- maker, Bank Quay, fined 55; Harop Chadwick, labourer, Church-street, fined 51 (fourth-time) ; Edward Morris, glass- maker, Wakefield-street, fined ss; John Daniels, glassmaker, Glass House-row, fined ss; Isaac Haesou, galvanizer, Chor- ley-street, boy ordered to receive twelve strokes with the birch ; and John Hardman, wiredrawer, Orford-lane, fined ss. TUESDAY.—Pefors Councillor C. Broadbent. DRLNKENNESS.—M.rgaret Meehan, fustian cutter, 18. Blackhurst-street, was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Mersey-street. She was dismissed en promising net to offend again. WEDNESDAY.—Bef ore Mr. John Fairclough. DRUNIC AT LATCHFORD.—Thomas Conway, Latchford, was fined 20s, including costs, or 14 days' imprisonment, for being drunk and disorderly in Knutsford-road. THURSDAY—Before Major Litton. The business is repelled elsewhere. FRlDLY.—Before the Mayor _(Alderman Ilarriaon), Alderman

Chandley, and Mr. John White. SLREPING OCT.—Wiiiiam Lawle-, Jane Flynn, and Mary Shields, were charged with sleeping in an unoccupied house in Rose-yard at 2 30 the same morning.—They were each sent to prison for fourteen
GENERAL NEWS.
----- Sir William Armstrong is establishing large steel works

in the vicinity of Naples. Mr. Chamberlain was sufficiently well on Saturday to travel from Ipswich to London. Mr. SIMUeI Morley, M.P., has sent a donation of £5 to the Prayer Book Revision Society. Mr. W. W. B. Beach, M.P , will next month open a new Masonic Lodge at the Soldiers' Institute, Portsmouth, to be conducted on total abstinence principles. Jane Johnson, of Leeds, who obtained notoriety from the number of her incarcerations for drunkenness, which exceeded 200, died in the Leeds Workhouse on Saturday,

aged 85. At Boughrood, Radnorshire, on Saturday evening, a rail- way porter took up a gun, and at the same time remarked to a fellow porter hamed Davies, " Look our, Charlie, I'll shoot you!" The gun went off, killing Davies on the spot. All the Ministers except Earl Spencer and Mr. Cham- berlain attended a Cabinet Council on Tuesday. Mr. 61adstone, who had travelled from liawarden, lookei very

well. CHESTER AS A PORT.—The Conservancy Board which is to replace the River Dee Company has resolved to promote, a bill in Parliament under which provisions will be made for rendering Chester a first-class port for the coasting ; trade. DOMESTIC TRAGEDY.—g: man named Peter M'Laelin, Cowcaddens, Glasgow, was found unconscious on Tueedry morning beside a splintered paraffin lamp. His wife is charged with throwing it at bins. ISPLaclin died on Tues- day afternoon. At a meeting of the Shropshire Chamber of Agricul- ture, on Seturdy, the question of Fair Trade was dis- cussed, fled while it was agreed that universal Free Trade was desirable, an addendum that pressure should be put upon protected countries to bring it about was not supported. The Citizen states :—The death of the Earl of Aylesford at so early an age as 35 will be a severe blow to most of the British offices. Insurances, amounting in all to a vast sum, have from time to tima been accepted upon his life, and there are very few companies in which he was not covered to a full extent. FRAUDS OF CLERKS —A man named John James Hum- phrey was convicted on Monday at the Central Criminal Court of having committed frauds on commercial clerks by means of advertisements offering situations, and was sen- tenced to five years' penal servitude. Although the prisoner is only 33 years of age, he had been engaged in the mal- practices for many years. A German White Book has been issued relating to the claims of Germany to land in the Fiji Isl ends. The claims were first formulated by Germany on the annexation of the Fiji Islands by England, and it was then proposed that those claims should be submitted to a Mixed Commission. This propcoal was res:sted for some years, but was finally agreed ti last year. MR, FORSTER, M.P., AND HIS CONSTITUENTS —Mr. W. E. Forster has issued an address to the electors of Bradford, in which he says :—" At the next general election I must either give up hope of being member for Bradford, or I must offer myself as candidate for one of its divisions. Under these circumstances I beg to state that I shall hope to solicit the suf- frages of the central division." LORD ENNISKILLEN, Imperial Grand Master of the Orange Society, hes issuel an address to the Oraegemen and Loyalists of Ireland, in which he contrasts their de. meannor with that of the Nationalists, and says it is time for their rulers to recognise the fact that each fresh sacri- fice on the shrine of disloyalty has only whetted the appe- tite of England's remorseless enemies. BARNUSI AND THE Cnareleanr.—The Tichborne claimant, in a letter to Mr. John de Morgan, published in the Toronto Weekly News, s iys :—" Could you oblige me by seeing Mr. Barnum, and ask him what he would guarantee me for a six months' tour through America with his circus, as I am en- tirely dependent on what I earn to keep my children, who I should have with me if I visited America" Mr. Barnum repliel by sayirg Sir Roger would not prove attractive in the United States. EXECUTION AT GALWAY.—At Galway, on Tuesday, Thomas Parry was hanged for the murder of a young ledy, to whom he was engaged, in August last. The execution had been postponed for a week in order that Parry's mental condition might be ascertained. Two medical gentlemen engaged by the Lord Lieutenant found that the convict was sane; but in a confession written an Monday night he as- serted that his mind was "not right" when he shot the young lady. Berry was the executioner. GREAT FIRES.—EXTENSM DAMAGE.—The malesion Of Sunlaws, Roxbnrgshire, the property and residence of Wm. S. Kerr, was entirely destroyed by fire on Friday. The fire broke out at four ann. above a bedroom occupied by the daughter of Lord Lee, who was a visitor. The damage is estimated at £2s,ooo.—The large bacon factory of Mr. J. White, High-street, Cralley Heath, Rowley, was destroyed. by fire on Tuesday, The fire broke out in the drying rooms, and owing to the scarcity of water the flames spread with great rapidity, and the building was completely gutted, the roof coming in with a great crash. The amount of damage is very large, and is partially covered by insu- rance. A YEAR'S RAILWAY ACCIDENTS.—Returns have been issued of accidents and casualties on the railways of the United Kingdom, reported to the Board of Trade, during the nine months ending September 30th, 1884. The total num- ber of persons killed was 859. and the number injured 5,832. Of these numbers 31 passengers were killed and 558 injured by accidents to trains, rolling stock, or permanent way ; 77 were killed and 487 injured by accidents from other causes. Of companies' servants 21 were killed and 83 in- jured by accidents to trains, rolling stock, 3:.;;.; and 374 were killed and 1,660 injured by accidents from other causes; 44 persons were killed and 23 injured at level crossings; 254 trespassers (including suicides) were killed and 136 in- jured. THE UNEMPLOYED OF THE METROPOLIS —A meeting of the unemployed, to consider the depression in the condition of the industrial classes, was held on Saturday afternoon in front of the Royal Exchange, London, Mr. W. Saunders presiding. Mr. Hennessy proposed "That the ever-recur- ring depression in trade, the chronic poverty of the indua- trial classes, and the difficulty of finding work, even at starvation wages, are intolerable evils, which ought not to be tamely endured by those who suffer from them, and can- not safely be ignored by any class in the nation." The re- solution was seconded by the Rev. Fleming Williams, and carried with only two dissentients. The Rev. Stewart 'Lleadlam moved, and Mr. Pike seconded, "That these evils are the result of the denial of the equal rights of men to the elements provided by their creation for the empleyment of labour, and we pledge ourselves in every way to impera- tively demand the restitution to the whole people of their birthright in the land." The resolution was adopted. Mr. Henry George said it was time the men in the streets and workshops took up this question. There was slight inter- ruption, but no disturbance. Mn. CAINE ON TEMPERANCE IN THE NAVY.—On Saturday evening Mr. Caine, M.P., Civil Lord of the Admiralty, pre- sided at Exeter Hall, London, at the cheap concert for the people given by the National Temperance League.—Mr. Caina referred to what he described as the gratifying pro- gress of temperance in the navy, and said that no organisa- tion had done so much to improve the moral and physical condition of seamen as the National Temperance League. He had tried in the House of Commons to net certain con- cessions made to the total abstainers, and when he went down to Scarborough for re-election, not long ago, his op- ponents asked the question of the electors—" Will you vote for a man who is going to rob poor Jack of his grog?" Their reply was to return him again by a large majority. (Applause.) He explained then, as he should like to do now, that he had never proposed to "rob Jack of his grog," , but to give him every facility to relinquish it voluntarily and to become a total abstainer. Compulsory temperance would be a great mistake. All he wished was that the argument for teetotalism might be brought before the men of both services, and that they might be left to judge for themselves. MURDER AND SUICIDE IN COUNTY DUBLlN.—lnteligence reached Dublin on Monday evening of a terrible occurrence which was discovered on Senday night at Garristown, a village in the county Dublin, within the Balbriggan police district. It would appear that a house and some 25 acres of land close to Garristosvn were held by a middle-aged man named Nicholas Aspell. He was unmarried, and a woman named Mary Connell kept house for him. The relations that existed between him and this woman were the subject of comment amine the neighbours. and it was understood that the two were shortly about to be married. It was noticed on Sunday that the house was shut up, and as the day wore on this circumstance caused remark. The police were communicated with, and they burst in the door of the house, when a sight was presented of a most shocking character. Stretched on her back on the floor, dead, lay the woman Connell. Her throat was cut, and it was evident She had been the victim of a brutal murder. Close to her was stretched the body of Nicholas Aspell, also dead and cold. He, evidently the murderer, had fallen on his face, and in his hand was clutched the.dagger with which the crime had been committed. Aspell had also cut himself about the threat. SIR CHARLES DILKE A.T BRADFORD—Sir Charles Mk° attended the annual soiree of the Chamber of Commerce at Bradford, on Monday evening, and delivered an address, dealing chiefly with the subject of commercial treaties and tariffs. He referred With satisfaction to the fact that Spain had now eneaged to replace British trade on the tooting of the most-favoured nation treatment, so that we ceuld again compete freely with the products of all other foreign countries in the Spanish market. The intolerable inconvenience of the past differential treatment was now fully recognised in Spain. He hoped that the object of ex- tending the markets for our goods might be promoted by such international agreement as was now under discussion at Berlin with regard to the Congo. The negotiations for simplifying the tariff arrangements in Turkey were making satisfactory progress. The long-continued negotiations with Mexico had resulted in the conclusion of the prelim- inary agreement for the renewal of friendly relations, which had now come into operation. Negotiations were also pro- ceeding for the corclusion of a treaty. In referring to the woollen trade, Sir Charles said last year's figures showed that Yorkshire need not fear foreign competition. He was not one of those who gave the smallest countenanca to the doctrine of Protection. GOVERNMENT OF INDIA-Mr. E, A. Navigation through the SUEZ Canal was suspended on Tuesday owing to a tempest. At the Lancaster assizes on Thursday a young fellow named Patrick M'Clurk, convicted of a violent assault, core.. A charge of from 61 to £1 was made for admiss:on; notwithstanding which the house was crowded in all parte Mr. Parnell said he looked forward to the future with a light heart, for he was convinced that five hundred thousand Irishmen enfranchised by the new Act would be even truer to Ireland than those who went before them. lllvilrg briefly touched on the land and labour ques- tion, he referred to that of Irish independence. They could not, he said, ask for lass than the restoration of Grattan's Parliament and its privileges. They could not under the British ConsWution ask for more; but no man had a right to fix the boundary of the march of the nation.

div.head: EXAMINER. SA TURDAY, JANUARY 24, DM.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SA TURDAY, JANUARY 24, DM.
Xetters to the editor.
CONVERTE.D INFIDELS.

Sir,—Last Sunday afternoon I visited the Public Hall with the object of seeing Slater, who has been announced as a converted Infidel. After being introduced as one who had been a disciple of Mr. Bradlaugh, Mr. Slater informed the audience, which was a very large one, that for ten years he had lectured up and down London in various clubs, against Christianity, and that eventually he was converted lat a Snlvation meeting to the cre:d he had denied. Now, on the authority of Mr. Bradlaugb, and with his permission to make this statement. I am enabled to say that this is ab- solutety false, for Mr. Slater has never been a Freetbought lecturer in London or anywhere else,and a& for his Infidelity or A.theism, as I prefer to call it.it is an easy matter for a man, wise apparently has little or no regard for the truth, to make pretensions of Atheism and then to be cmverted. It would pay both himself and "General " Booth, as, by attracting such audiences as that which filled the Hall on Sunday, the collection boxes are soon filled. My reason for writing this is that I may show those who listened to this man's harangue on Sunday and believed him to be a bona- file convert, that both they and Booth's simple-minded followers have been gulled. Of those members of the Sal- vation Army who had him down here, I would say, "forgive them, they know not what they do."—Yonrs, Szc., AN UNCONVERTED INFIDEL.

div.head: 'FUR PROFITS!'
div.p: 'FUR PROFITS!'

Sir,—l have read with intereet the letter in your paper signed " Fair Profit," but I fear that until our social sys- tem is very much altered permanently fair profits will be the exception and not the rule. I believe the wealth of this country is enormously greater than it was a century ago, but have those parties or their predecessors who are in posseaion of the increased amount of wealth been the pro- ducers of that increase ? Competition is so close and keen , that manufacturers generally have great difficulty and much anxiety in making tbtir works pay, and when im- provements are made the recipients of the greatest amount of benefit arising from those improvements are most fre- quently the aristocracy and the mmied class, while the great bulk of the people continue to struggle fearfully hard for life, honesty, independence, and honour, which only the moot fortunate and the strongest succeed in maintaining. The law e affecting land and excessive population cause the existence of an idle, extravagant, and fre- quently profligate aristocracy, pauperism, and crime. To sustain these the profits of our manufacturers are ab- sorbed and the wages of the working classes lowered. They are the imperfections of our social organisation, which we should try to remedy, for they rob the nation of ita pros- perity and the people cf their comfort and pleasure. May I add that when poverty and misery are not the results of vice—
To help a.,,d sympathise with human we Is what the hapvy to the unhappy owe. —Yours, Ake., S KEN YON.

div.head: TEETOTALISM IN EARLESTOWN.
div.p: TEETOTALISM IN EARLESTOWN.

Sir,—lt was my lot to hear the moderation sermon preached in the Wesleyan Chapel on Temperance Sunday. When I heard the minister announce his text, which was "Therefore with joy shall ye draw water' out of the wells of salvation," knowing his general p-oclivity, I thought he would stick tenaciously to his text and preach a purely " water " sermon, naively avoiding any mention of temper- ance. This would have b:en the most politic course for him to pursue. But he mixed his potion with strong drink, evidently ietoxicating his hearers, some with delight and others with disgust. As a member of the Wesley-an Society I was sorry that the sermon was delivered, and do now sin- cerely deplore the discussion which has arisen through it. Why should the c netroyersy be carried on any further? If it wan likely to do any good it wru'd be welcome; but I do not see the likelihood. It has been undertaken in an an- tagonistic spirit, each disputant is pre-determined to keep his stand let whatever argument en:le that, may, and the original subject will in the end have to be left where it was found. It breeds illfeeling and hi s the mischievous ten- dency of separating Chrietian workers, thus grievously rend- ing the 'mystic body of Christ." One church in the neighbourhood has been brought to a lamentable state through dissensions which sprang from a very trivial matter; then let us take warning in time. It means also a waste of time and energy. There is a story to the effect that two sheep once came across a splendid tuft of grass at the same time, a prolonged struggle took place between them for the possession of it, this, taking them aside from the sweet morsel, allowed easy access to it for a third, who munched away till it was all gone: so that whether there was a vic!or in the combat or net, there was certainly no prize. "Disgusted Moderator" and "Disgusted Teeto- taller" both express deep concern for the drunkard, but how will they feel if they find that, while wrangling in print, they have missed the opportunity of holding out a warning hand to the besotted wretch as he stumbled along to an untimely and a hopeless grave? It is bad to indulge a spirit of strife, and worse to neglect opportunity of doing good. Do they each pretend to have the certain cure for drunkenness? Let them test the value of their separate claims by practic illy applying them in the Case of drunkards, and then the public will accord to give its hear- tiest welcome to the publication of their success. Hoping that I have not added more fuel, I am, sir, yours, 4±c WESLEYAN.

Sir,—Will you kindly allow ma a portion of your space Bo that I may say a few words upon this" burning ques- tion." • I see the Liberation Society has determined to make fresh efforts towards liberating the people from the most oppressive and galling subjection in which they are held by this priestly caste, It is quite the fashion now-a-days to deprecate anything like strong language. am sure the teetotallers of Eulestown will be extremely obliged to " Constant Reader " in yours of last week, for his kind fatherly advice. Had he been more neutral and not so touch one-sided the advice would have come with a better grace. That the discussion is becoming in some quarters a mere word controversy cannot but be admitted, but the teetotallers are not wholly to blame for that. The first words certainly came from "Disgusted Teetotaller," but they only amounted to six or eight lines put in the form of a question. This elicited a short but concise reply in the Exanzi,tee from "Moderator," and a very much longer, wordy, and blustering, but less argumentative reply in your contemporary signed " A Disgusted Moderator.'" These were replied to through your columns by " Disgusted Teetotaller," whose remarks were not worthy a reply, and another from " Tee Tee," who dealt only with a Modera- tor' e " letter. Since then we have had replies from various correspondents, more or less wordy. But, of course, it is our teetotal friends only who have got astray and whoshould unite in a friendly spirit in attempting to put down evil of all kinds, which is what they are trying to do constantly. Now, if 1 this discussion can only be conducted in a reasonable manner —and it ought to be—good will certainly come out of it, but if it is allowed to continue quite away from the ques- tion at issue, and Into personal animosity and feelings, then the sooner it comes to an end and the better for all sectiens of the community. The real question seems to me to be— not merely whether Christ was a teetotaller or not, but also whether total abstinence principles are in accord with the teachings of the Bible or not. To my mind this is what both' Moderator " and "Tee Tee " are aiming at, and I hope they will both set a good example by sticking to the I question.

In conclusion, I cl'ould strongly Ncominend your corres- pondents to discuss the question without any further refer- ence to either the source that has led to the discussion or to any denomination whatever, it having now become a public question. Above all, avoid all personalities, or as " Tee Tee " puts it. confine yourselves t) reason, argument and tact, not sneering, or rancour, or vulgar abuse. My advice to " Disgusted Teetotallers ". and " Moderators " is he reasonable and take the above advice, or put your pens and papers into your desks and leave them there, and so save time and expense of what is not worth setting the type for. —I am, sir, one who in all good things, but especially language, would counsel MODERATION. Earlestown,2oth January, 1385. [We have several other letters on this question for which we cannot find room, and would suggest that our correspon- dents leave the matter to " Moderator " on the one side and " Tee Tee" on the other.—Em.

old bottle. Certain particles of its former contents stuck to the insides of the wine-skins after being emptied ; and becoming exposed to the atmosphere, germs of the yeast plant were formed, so that if new wine were poured into the old bottle, fermentation would at once begin, carbonic acid gas would be generated, and the bottle, however strong it might be, would burst asunder through the very great pressure. Yermented wine, on the other band, might with safety be put into old bottles. If new wine is put into new leather bottles, no fermentation would be communi- cated, and the air being carefzlly excluded, both the new wine and the new bottles would be preserved. And now, sir, when I mike a request for bread, it is not very pleasant to be offered a stone. I asked " Moderator " to give us facts, and he answers by citing authorities ; I would ask him to read my last letter again. I wish to point out to "Moderator" that it is not only to "Tee Tee" he is writing, and fOr whom his facts and argu- ments are required, but the whole community. Ile and I— with a few other correspondents—are only representatives of two large parties who are deeply interested. The points reNrred to by his authorities, which were raised by "Moderator" himself, I leave for his farther con- sideration.

And now, in conclusion, I most say I was rather astonish-- ed, after going through his letter, to read that" Moderator's"' position is an impregnable one, a veritable Gibraltar rock that cannot be moved. However, that remains to be proved yet, no. serious attempt having being made so far. Again, I affirm that true teetotallers are afraid of no battle- ground.

If " Moderator" says that anywhere in the Bible, there is Divine sanction associated with the use of intoxicating drinks, let him show it. Haying opened the discussion, as I before stated, it is clearly the day of "Moderator." er others. of his party,. to prove their position. As abstainers we do not in the first nstance appeal to the Bible. Science and ex- pelience have taught us the evils of drinking, and are every day vindicating the wisdom and utility of abstinence principles.—l am, dear sir, yours respectfully, " TEE,III,E." 15411Janu try, 1885
