Sir,—l see from your 1-a-si-i-s-s-ue the the clerk, appears to have monopolised all the talk, in accord tnce with his cue- torn, at the last meeting of the School Board. It has been suggeseed to me, and I certainly agree with tho remark, that I he is perfectly pachydermatous. As usull, teo, when spe Or- ing of Trinity boys' school, he uttered two or three inac- curacies which with your permission I wish to rectify. It is not a fact, for instancer.that the average attendance in I any part of May, 1831 or 1884 was either 243 or 253 I sea by reference to my books that the clerk quoted the num- ber on the rolls in each case. Surely he didn't do it to prove ' his staternent—n very different thing to average attendance. The average attendance for May, 1891 was 191, and for the corresponding month in 1884 it was 219, an increase of 28. By reducing this to a percentage the average attendance in May, 1884, is fully 8 per cent better than in 1881. The system of charging increased fees did not come into force in May, 1881, as the clerk insinuates; the managers' resolution bears date 4th September, 1882. For this latter year the buys' average was 212, for last year 230, an in- crease of 18 ; resulting largely from imposition of increased fees. I think these facts demolished the misrepresentation respecting our attendance. I will, however, go just a step further and state that under my regime the average attendance at Trinity boys' school bas increased 71 with almost identical numbers on the books. It is not true that our increased grant "is ow- in in a large measure to the generosity of the I Legislature." As a rule the Legislature only pay schools what they earn (in several cases they even reduce the earnings, thus proving, I suppose, generosity) and the earnings are much more difficult to get now than formerly. Neither is it a fact that the Government grant is double what it was formerly. Under the old cude the Government offered 19s as capitation money ; now it offers £1 Os 10d (in each case without specifics). The latter sum methinks, is about Is 101 in excess. Under what I will call the 193 Code the limitation of payment was 17s 6], and under the " Mundella Code" the most that can be obtained (unless the school be favourably circumstanced in respect of sub- scriptions) is 178 6d. If these amounts ba subtracted and the answer multiplied by 243, 233, or any other number in fact, I fail to find any mathematical process by which the result £l6l can be obtained. £l6l is the difference between

last year's grant and that awarded rive years ago. The fact is, sir, that increased grant Is only attainable now-a-days by good average attendance, good in:thod, awfully and constant bard work, much patience and self-denial on the part of parents, teachers, and scholars. By combining many of these virtues last year, we succeeded in placing our school (for the first time in its his'ory) in the honourable position of suffering a reduction in the grant of £32 14s 9d, that being the total excess of the 17s 61 limit upon average attendance.—Yours faithfully, T. EL NNETT.
THE CHURCH OF ENGLAND.

;worth fighting for, the people were subject in every sense to the rule of the priestly bigot. To call Laud a martyr is V, turn history upside down. As to the king's adviser, he urged violent and repressive measures, and as an ambitious prelate, he made himself intolerable. Working hand in hand with Strafford, he paved the way for all recent Irish disaffection. As a powerless- old priest, he might, at seventy years old, have been allowed to die in peace, but it is the essence of priestcraft that it clings tenaciously to thin- world's goods so long as life exists. We have an example of this nearer home and ;Ti,our own day. The rev. gentle ruin is nevertired of harping on the question that the Church always looked after the welfare of the people. When the first grant of £30,000 was-proposed by the Government for , educational purposes, it was regarded as the narrow end of a dangerous wedge by many,..especially by those who dreaded', the strengthening of anrinfinenee not exercised by them— selves. The Church party called a meeting in the Corn Exchange, Manches'er. Canon Wray presided, and the Rev. Hugh Stowell was, the leading speaker. A body ef working-men, favourable tonational education, having taken the matter into consideration,decided that their views should,. be represented. To this end each of them agreed to go to one of the shops where the tickets for the meeting were to- be had, and get as many as they could. In this way they secured considerably Own one half the tickets, and quietly distributed them amongetetheir fellows in certain large work- shops, with instructions to attend in their go.to-meeting clothes." They did se;. and to the astonishment of the ' rev, chairman, and his leading speakers, negatived all the resolutions which were- pat against State aid to education. This is but one sample out of scores that could be given . where the Establishnrent has tried all within its power to ! keep education from the people. How do church school. in Warrington compare- with the school at Bank Quay PY In one you have to quietly present a testimonial, and get rid of ' the teacher. In the ethers it is the open boast of, the scholars that if they can only •• pass" in scriptures, they t needn't bother about anything else. This state of, 'things will continue so long as mm are at the head of the same mental calibre as 11L'r. Carleton. W. ASP.

div.p: EARLESTOWN.

• NEW LOCAR MAGISTRATE —At the Liverp.4ol Quar- ter Sessions on Tuesday, Mr. Frederick Williatn.Gooch, of Mount Villa, Wargrave, took the oath and was. qualified as a justice of the peace for the county of lancaster. Mr. Gooch has ksenly interested himself in mattersaSecting the well-beings.! Earlestown and Newton, and fur some years has occupied the position of chairman of the Board of Im- provement Commissioners for the township of Newton. This, coupled with his connection with the Vulcan Foundry Company, will clues the announcement of his elevation to the magisterial bench to be received with general satisfac- tion throughout the district.

MISCELLANEOUS ENTERTAINNENT. An Entertain- I meat of an enjoyable character was given in the Good Templars' lodge-room, Bridge street, Earlestown, on Satur- dayjevening, under the auspices of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars. There was a fair attendance, and Brother John Taylor, W.C.T., occupied the chair. After the opening ode had been sung, recitations were given by Brothers G. E. Warburton and John Warburton; readings by Brothers E. Newman' A. W. Kenyon, and J. Barnard, and songs by Sister Whitty, Brothers J. Taylor, William Welker, and Miss Jackson. Brother Jos. James gave selec- tions on a dulcimer.

NEWSROOM FOR TUE BOTTLE WORKS. —By the kind- neas of Messrs. Borron and Little, of the Bottle Works, Crow-lane, the hands employed by the firm have been pro. vided with a capitkl newsroom. One of the workshops was utilised for the purpose, and was divided into two compart- ments; the largest portion being used as the newsroom, and the other as a draughts, chess, and dominoe room. Mr. Little has been appointed ptesident, Mr. Rylands vice-presi- dent, and the institution is managed by a committee of 13 persons, with Mr. Mosscroft secretary. About 130 persons sat down at the opening tea party, which was held in the newsroom on Saturday week; and at the subsequent pro- oeedings the chair WAS occupied by Mr. Rylands, vice- president. Song's were given by several of the workmen, and at the close a beady vote of thanks was accorded to Messrs. Borron and Little for their kindness in granting the use of the room.

TILER VIILOAN S/C1 AND ACC/DENT VI:IND.—The an- nual meeting of the members of the Vulcan Sick and Burial Club, an institution established in connection with the Vul- can Iron Foundry, for the benefit of the workmen em- ployed thereat, was held in the dining hall at the works on Saturday afternoon. There was a comparatively good at- tendance, and considerable interest appeared to be mani- fested in the proceedings. The chair was occupied by Mr. Jas. Creed, chairman of the committee of management. Officers for the ensuing year were nominated ; Mr. James Cowie being appointed chairman in place of Mr. Creed. Other business was transacted after which a discussion took place on the working of the society, and some dissatisfaction was exPressed in connection therewith. Illtitnatelv a reso- lution was proposed that the society be dissolved, and this was carried almost unanimously. The opinion of the whole body of members will be taken by means of the ballot upon the question of disealving the society
_ ANTI - VACCINATION MBETING AT EABLESTOWII. - A

specially-convened meeting, by circular, of the members And friends of the Earlestown branch of the Anti-Compul- sory Vaccination Society was held in one of the rooms of I Welcome Coffee Palace, Market-place, Earleetown, on Satur- I day afternoon. There was a comparatively good attendance, and Mr. John Clarke presided. It was explained that the meeting had been celled to consider the election of a Guar- dian to fill the vacancy in the representation of Newton township on the Warringten Board of Guardians, and the advisability of nominating a candidate who would repre- sent the views of the anti-vaccinationists of the district. Among those who took part in the meeting were Messra W. Girmour, B. Harrison, Garnett, A. Forster, and others, and a general feeling seemed to be entertained by those present that as the anti-vaccinationists bad been the means of bring- ing the election about, they were perfectly testified in nomi- rating a candidate. It was ultimately decided that Mr. John Clarke should be nominated for the vacant post. THE RECENT RECEPTION OP THE STANLEY TEAM AT EARLESTOWN.—Since the discreditable conduct of a number of Earlestown lads and supporters of the Earlestown Wanderers' club, on the occasion of the second match be- tween that team and the Liverpool Stanley,- when the latter received a somewhat " warm" reception, the matter has occasioned considerable talk in football circles in South West Lancashire. A short time ago the Stanley club brought the matter before the committee of the Liverpool and Dis- trict Football Association by lodging a formal complaint as to the manner in which they were treated on their visit to Earlestoven. The Stanley team alleged that they were met by a mock - band led by a member of the committee, and tbat they were threatened with per- sonal violence if they happened to win the match. The complaint was that the committee of the Earlestown club did not attempt to put a atop to the unseemly behaviour. 1 The committee of the Association expressed the opinion that the committee of the Earlestown Wanderers club was respon- sible for the decent behaviour of their supporters, and passedl a resolution that in the event of such proceedings happening in the future they would feel it their duty to take more stringent measures to put a stop to them. NEWTON, AND THE REDISTRIBUTION BlLL.—Little or no interest is being manifested by the inhabitants of Earles- town and Newton at the prospect of the last-named place being appointed the centre of one of the new electoral divi- sions of Semth-Weat Lancashire under the Redistribution of Seats BM The Government scheme, as proposed by the Boundary Commissioners, includes in the Newton division the parishes of Culcheth, Ashton-in-Makerfield, and Rain- hill, the Petty Sessional divisions of St. Helens and War-

rington, and Part of the municipal borough of Warrington, I the population of the district being 51,201. To the heads of the political parties in South-West Lancashire the general scheme has occasioned great dissatisfaction, as it is quite contrary to the schemes suggested by them. The representatives of the two political parties were at one in thinking that it would be advisable to group together into one district the large colliery districts of Ashton-in-Makerfield, Haydock, Newton, Golborne, Skelmersdale, and Rainford, which together with the scattered agricultural district in the south-east would make a compact division with a pepulation of over 60,000. But it is proposed by the Commissioners to take away a part of the northern portion of the coalfield, adding Skel- mersdale to Ormskirk, which is purely an agricultural dis- trict. and to the district proposed by both parties they have added the township of Culchsth, which properly belongs te Leigh. In order to form the Ince district the Commissioners have talmn from the Newton district, suggested by the two political parties, the townships of Billinge and Winstanley. The scheme is somewhat unsatisfactory to both parties, as it ignores the natural convenience of the districts in which the great populations reside, and it is stated that it will be strongly opposed before the Commissioners.

Sitserman Dnowtsrwu Cesk.—Shortly after three o'clock on Monday afternoon, as two men named William Hill and Joseph Unsworth (residents of Warrington), in the employ of the London and North. Western Railway Corn-- pany,,were working a "dredge boat" In the Sankey canal, near Newton Common Lock, they discovered the dead body of a man standing upright in the water. It was thereupon got to the side and conveyed to the Ship Inn (kept by My& Hayes), and information was given to the police. The body was subsequently identified as that af Henry John Bishop, 28A3rears of age, who was formerly employed as a labourer at the Sankey Sugar Works, and 7:colded with his father-in- ' law at 42, Bank-street, Etrlestown. Inquiries were f ore wards instituted, and it was ascerhined that the poos fellow had been missing since the Sib- December. On that day he went to his work in the morning, but returned in-the after-1 noon and complained to hin sister that he could < not follow his employment owing te his band, which wausone. He partook of his dinner, changed his olothing, and left his lodgings, for the purpose of taking'a walk, about four o'clock in the afternoon.. The decessed ited the Ship Inn about eight o'clock at night and remained nntil shortly after half-past ten,liusing which time he- had two or three glasses of ale. On Leaving the house ho stated that he was going to his lodgings, but he never arrived there. His whereabouts subsequently remained a mystery until the dis- covery of his body as stated. There is no, suspicion of foul play. The face and front portion of the body was thickly coated with mud, and the deceased was fully dressed. The locks and the " wash " running alongside are well protected by railings, and to reach the spot where the body was found the deceased must have gone to the extreme end of the railings and a little way into an adjOining field before reach- ing the water. It is said he was perfectly sober when tie left the Ship Inn, The night; however, was very darh,

WARRINGTON Lll3 ER AL ASSOCIATION. MR. W. CROSFIELD, J.P., ON FAIR TRADE. On Tuesday evening the annual meeting of the General Council of the above aseocietion was held at the Liberal dab, Bewsey-street. In the absence of Mr. Mclelinnies, DI.P., the chair was occvpied by Alderman Burgess. There was a large attendance. The following officers were elected, viz. :—Preeldent, Mr. S. Rigby, J.P. Vice-presidents : Mr. J. G. McMinnies, M.P. ; Mr. G. Croefield, J.P. ; Alderman Burgess, J.P. ; Mr. F. Monks, J.P. ; Hon. treasurer : Mr. John Croefield, J.P. A resolution was unanimously adopted in favour of the bill about to be introduced into Parlia- ment by Mr. Hopwood, M.P. for Stockport, to make affirms- tian permissible in piece of an oath. Some discussion took place with respect to the action of the railway com- ranies to raise their rates, and ultimately the matter was referred to the subcommittee. Subsequently Mr. Wm:rem Cnosoreen, who was warmly received, addressed the meeting. Before he touched upon tee subject he intended to speak upon he wished to say how glad he bad been to bear the discussion on the question of oaths. He entirely agreed with what had been said by the various speakers on that subject. From his own prac- tical experience, sitting in one of the busiest courts in the kingdom, he knew of the extremely slovenly and even dis- graceful way in which the administration of the oath wee =ducted, and the disregard which seemed to be paid to the oath when administered. (Hear, hear) They were all of teem familiar with the fact that there were certain classes who had been exempted from the oath Qnakers, in whom 11-, John Crosfield and himself were particularly interested, had for many generations been allowed to make a declara- tion in the way which suited their consciences best. Their " aye" was accepted as" aye," and their nay" as " nay." (Hear, hear.) lie found that recently even clergymen had been allowed to set aside the oath under certain circum- stances and to make declarations Even in his short expe- rience. of magisterial work, he had noticed that there was a decided tendency to diminish the occasions upon which oaths are subscribed to; and in the matter of official (loc- i:mints which required attesting very few people made a declaration in the form of an •oath, but almost everybody was allowed to make a declaration in the civil form. He thought that method might be very well extended to the other matters embraced in their resolution. (Hear, hear.) tt had been urged that the Liberals should constantly ad- Tecate freedom of worship, and that that freedom ought to be extended still further. (Hear, hear.) They desired that every man should be at liberty to worship as they liksd, or if a man did not desire to worship the matter was between his own conscience and his God. (Hear. hear) He thought they would all agree with him that it was a matter which individuals kept very much in their own heads, and the complaint of the churches certainly had been for some time that they took it too much in their own hands, (Hear, hear, and laughter.) They had at any rate the ability to stop away if they did not wish to conform to other people's views. (Laughter.) The subject he was going to speak upon was one which seemed to be an exceedingly wide question and on that account he had put it aside when selecting subjects upon which to address War- rington audiences, rather from a fear that he could not compress it into reasonable limits. He alluded to the ques- tion of Fair Trade. He found that it was being much more Carefully considered, and that it was even being lifted out of the realms of petty politics. (Hear, bear.) It was of course a political queetion, but it was almost ceasing to be a party politicel question, and from being looked at fairly from both sides it was losing very much of the gigantic dimensions it had possessed some time since, and was being treated much more calmly than it was some year or two ago. The cry for fair trade was one which they heard con- stantly when trade became bad, which they would know did not appertain to any one political body. All Governments alike bad to experience bad trade. They knew that it used to be said that every ten years there was bad trade, but the period was gradually being reduced and it was now every nine years that they suffered. Whenever these depressions of trade came they had cries that England was very much worse off than her neighbours, and that this country was suffering more than any. other country. This was the case some few years ago when the agricultural interest was suf- fering mainly through there having been a series of years of exceedingly bad weetlitr. There was a gentleman in the House of Commons who was peculiarly fitted to advocate the farmers' side of the question and be was made one of the Royal Commission which went abroad to inquire into the state of affairs in other countries particularly in Araerica. He noticed that the other day this gentleman—he referred to Mr. Clare Sewell Read— was waited upon and asked to take part in some fair trade demonstration, and he dealt with that subject in a shorter speech than he (Mr. Cresfield) intended to do. Mr. Read summed up the whole matter in the words "Fair Trade is humbug." (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Having next re- ferred to the speeth by Sir W. B. Forwood, in which that gentleman gave his experience of the working of a protective policy in the United States, and expressed an opinion ad- verse to Fair Trade, Mr. Croefield said that that question became a very big one if they dealt as sometimes was dealt with the matter of imports and exports. There were some who would tell them that when imports were in excess of ex- ports there was an exceedingly lamentable condition of affairs. He would borrow an illustration which showed the fallacy of this view. Mr. J. K Cross, under secretary for India, had spoken very weightily upon that matter and amongst other illustratione he give the following obe, which would show the fallacy more clearly than any other. He took the illustration of a cargo of coal which went from Cardiff to San Francisco, and which cost in the-first instance £l,OOO. The freighlt to Sin Francisco amounted to £1.500, se that the return which the buyer of the coal in San Fran- cisco WAS to give was £2,500. Grain was purchased to the extent of that £2,500 in payment of the coal. The freight of the grain was again £1.500, so that when the return for toot £l,OOO worth of goods cornea to be made say at Liverpool, the amount that is to be received is £l,OOO instead of tha £l,OOO which had been taken away. They would, see, therefore, that in that single transaction the amount of the original export was multiplied font times. (Hear, hear.) From illustrations of that kind they would see that there was -room for very large increases in their imports. and that they were certainly not the losers by transactions of that kind. (Applause.) To nut it simply, exports were what they paid, and imports were what they got for their money. He might bring the matter into narrower compass if they would allow hire to borrow one of their wives for an illus- tration. (Latrehter ) He Was following an old precedent in taking a working man's wife for such an illustration. In Atte Beek of Proverbs was given a ve. y grand description of a good wife, ao d. the writer of that book had considerable experience of women, and therefore they might take it as very valuable. (Laughter.) He told them that a "good , wile is like the merchant ships; she bringeth her food from ear." The way in which he should very respectfully treat this illustration was to point out that the wife, with the weekly wage, and with the market basket on her arm, car- ried the exports, and that the provisions which came beck from market after the expenditure of the week's wages were the imports. Now he thought there was no man in that 203 M who would grumble at the wife if she took away the weekly wages and brought back home provisions worth four times the money she had taken out. (Hear. hear.) Yet that was a case analogous to the case he had mentioned of the coal and the corn. There was certainly this fallacy about it, he could not carry the simile to the end, because the transaction he had just spoken of as to the wife and the provisions was very largely a ready money transaction—of paying across the counter. They did not need to be told that foreign trade was ye :y much a matter of barter. There was another illustration he should take which would point that out to them. They had an import- ant trade in Warrington—the trade in wire. Very large consumers of wire, such as that made in Warrington, were the ranches of South America, which need the wire for hurdling; but be thought none of them would expect that the payment for this wire which Warrington mana would he immediately returned to the wire maker by way of barter. They would hardly expect the wire works of Warrington to receive back direct the hides which catne from the Brazils. The hides, however, did come to Warrington, and they had the benefit Of them, though they came through a great many bands, and a great many profits were made oat of them. (Hear, heir.) Some people said that In order to have fair trade they must rake a bargain, one country with another, and say that if they will not take our goods we will not take their goods. That seemed very much like the shoemaker saying to the tailor "I will not buy my coat in your shop if you will not bur your shoes in my shop." (Laughter.) They should get- into a very unsatis- factory state of affairs if they restricted themselves in that way—(hear, hear)—but that was what the fair traders wanted them to do. But he maintained that that even could not he done. The circuitous character of trade entirely prevented it. If they were to pledge themselves against a Country and that country wanted their goods she would get them whether they would or not. In illustration of this, Mr. Crosfield pointed out that in Burrnah rice was very 1,1-feelY produced, and that country received large supplies ot mineral oil from the United States. These two articles were not exchanged in a direct mincer, but the rice was brought from Burmah to England, where it was dressed. It was then very largely re-exported to the island of Cuba, which was a large consumer of rice. Cuba produces large quantities of sugar, and as the United States do not produce sufficient of that article they import it from Cuba. Eng- land in turn was paid for the cleaned rice by bread-stuffs which come from New York to Liverpool and other ports. This kind of trade was going on all over the world. They could not have direct trades as they might wish them to be; and they could no more make trade flow in the channel which suited them than they could make Water run up-hill. Fair trade as he should like to see it understood was a good value for the commodities they exported, and he thought that was the only sound sense in Which fair trade could he underslool. (Applause.) He took it that it was the duty of England to set an example to other nations. It was an unselfish example, because he felt very Well satirfigl that if other nations adopted free trade princielee to the exteut England had they would then know for the first time whet real hard competition was. (Hear, hear.) Foreign manufacturers wore new fighting the battle with England with one hand tied behind their backs. When they got free trade that hand would be un- tied, and the English manufacturers would then know what a blow was when it came straight from the sho.ulder. They had first of all to secure all the benefits of free trade to their Own countrymen, then they had to display the bene.

THE SOUDAN CAMPAIGN. LATEST DETAILS. Vanity Fair says Lord Woiseley has had a fall from his camel, and is now detained at Korti in order to recover from the effects of it. The Central News says the uneasiness felt on Thursday in respect to Gen. Sfewart's position deepened into anxiety yesterday, when hour after hour passed without any word being received of the progress made by the advanced British force It is believed in official quarters that Gen. Stewart is now entrenched at Metemneh, and that no alarm need be felt at the absence of difinite intelligence to that effect, as the enemy is in such force in the locality that it would be highly dangerous for any but the strongest escort to make the journey across the desert to , Korti, and Gen^ral Stewart would not at the present juncture be likely to weaken his small force unless under the most urgent necestity. Many military officers called at , the War Office yesterday, and amongst other visitors was 1 Sir William Harcourt, who remained for some time in con- sultation with the permanent officials of the Department. The Duke of Cambridge and the Marquis of Hartington attended at the War Office late in the afternoon, and remained some time engaged upon official duties. Rumours were in circulation last night that General ; Stewart has been again attacked by the rebels, and is now surrsunded in the desert. The officials of the War Office have no information and discredit the report. FRENCH MILITARY SUCCESS. PARTS, FRIDAY.—The Minister of Marine has received the following telegram from M. Thomson, governor of Cochin China, dated Phunpehu, to-day :—The column under Lieutenant-Colonel Miramond surprised Sivotha in his camp at Mind, on the 21st mat, at 5 o'clock in the even- ing. The band were victoriously attacked, and completely dispersed, with. the loss of twenty killed.__

THE AVAL‘NCIIES IN ITALY.—GREAT LOSS OF LIFE. A Central News telegram, dated Rome, Friday morning, states : Fresh details of disaster arrive from the northern provinces. At Deveis, in Susa, the snow covers sixty dead. At Mentonlles, in the Finer°lo district, the church roof fell in from the terrible we,ght of snow accumulated upan it, burying many victims beneath it. Some of these unfortu- nate persons had taken refuge in the sacred building. At Chaumont the snow is eight yards deep. At the marble gtsarry of Foggera, twenty workmen_have been entombed in the snow, and in the same district a number of inhabitants have disappeared, having, it is believed, been buried. No less than 50 houses have been crushed by the snow. The work of rescue goes on indefatigably, and some thousands of soldiers and labourers are exerting themselves strenu- ously. -

Cans, at Hill Cliff e. That cause, historically speaking, was at Hill Cliffs one ef the most interesting to a dissenter that he could know of. Their cluse was one of the oldest dis- senting causes in England, and when it was established dis- senters lived different lives to what was the case now. In what ware called the "good old days" it was a dan- gerous thing to be a dissenter. In the days when men had to fight for the right to worship God according to the dic- tates of their conscience, •if a man conscien- tiously differed from the State church of that time and desired to worship according to his own views, he had to do it out of the sight of those ;whO were of a different cast of feeling to himself. Hs was hun- ted do ten and more harshly treated than now were the beasts that perish. With broader and more enlightened views those times had changed, but not without a struggle. The time came when they were tolerated as dissenters, but were not allowed the rights of citizens—except to pay taxes. (Laughter.) It was in the memory of most how the great universities were closed to the beet men in the country until quite recently. A man might at that time be the cleverest in the college or universities, but if he was a dissenter, he must when he had got to a certain point, either forswear his conscientious belief, or leave the College or University. He was glad that now Nonconformity was taking a proper position, with a result that none need be ashamed V. (Ap- plause ) But perfect equality was not yet gained. It was quite true that a great many privileges were now open to them, but conscientious dissenters believed that every religious faith and creed should stand upon its own bottom. (Applause.) Therefore he would impress upon them—es- peciallv young men—to study Carefully this country's his- tory of dissent, and if they were not strengthened in their religious convictions and raith, made better dissenters, and more determined to promote the ultimate issue—the perfect freedom of religion from State control—they were different men to what he took them for. (Applause.) The Chairman, tbe Revs. R. Yeatman, B. Moore, W. C. Taylor, and James McTurk then delivered brief addresses, spe eking in warm terms of Mr. Pilling's work and sterling character.—The following presentations were then made to Mr. Pilling :—An illuminated address, signed by over one hundred persons, presented by Mr. Goodier, on behalf of the signatories ' • a black marble timepiece, presented by Mr. Jepson, on behalf of the subscribers; a purse of gold, money collected and not expended on the presentations, presented by Mr. William Booth; a silver teapot, presented by Mr. B. Evans on behalf of Runcorn friends; a silver cruet stand and add rses, presented by Mr. Grounds on behalf of the teachers and scholars of the Sunday school ; a set of china, presented by Mr. Summer, on behalf of the ladies of the congregation. —Mr. PILLING, in reply, expressed his sincere thanks to his many friends for the manifestations of their regard.— A vote of thanks was accorded the presentation committee, on the motion of Mr. J. IVilkinson, seconded by Mr. J. Ken- worthy; Mr. Booth responded on behalf of the committee. —A vote of thanks was passed to those who had bad charge of the tea that TM given prior to the meeting, on the motion of Mr. G. Wallington seconded by Mr. Naylor. —Mr. Pilling proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman, and Mr. J. H. SPENCELEY, in seconding, said he hoped that Mr. Crosfield, the Liberal candidate for' Warrington, who went in for liberty and conscience in every denomination— (epplause)—would at the present and in the future do his utmost to carry out that liberty that all true Christians desired.—Mr. Wilkinson also spoke to the resolution, which was carried. In responding to the vote of thanks, Mr. YONGE said that he was always glad to render any assistance in his power to the friends at Hill Cliffe. He regarded them as the staunch adherents and representatives of Nocconformity in that locality. Mr. Roberts in his sneech had spoken of the com- parative ease with which a man could be a dissenter in these days. Yet, still many present would know from ex- perience that even now dissenters endured considerable per- secution and disability. He had heard, more than once, with considerable indignation, of petty meannesses and tyrannies pract'ced by proud churchmen not a hundred miles from that soot upon dissenters. When the children of dissenters were compelled to walk at the tail of the na- tienel school procession on a festival occasion, it still looked as if dissent meant snubbing and reproach. It was time that this was put a step to, and he hoped that all there would show that such conduct received their indignant pro- test. (Loud applause.) Mr. SPENCELRY rose to explain that the treatment of the children referred to by the chairman had arisen from an oversight. It had been arranged that all the children should walk with their Sunday school teachers, and et course as the dissenting teachers were not there, the dissenting chil- dren had to walk by themselves. He assured the meeting that the occurrence was only an oversight. The CHAIRMAN rejoined that he was glad he had men- tioned the matter, as it had elicited such an explanation. If, as Mr. Spencely said, the matter was an oversight, the chairdem trusted that the oversight would never occur again. (Renewed applause.) The meeting was terminated by the singing of the doxolcgy.

DISHONESTY AND AMUSEMENT —At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Thursday, before Alderman J. Harrison and Mr. C. J. Bishop, Robert Taylor, a lad 15 years of age, residing with his parents In Appleton-street, Peasley Cross, was Charged with stealing 1., the property of a labourer named Lock, living in the same street. It appears that the prose- cutor gave the lad a shilling with which to bey some coal, but instead of making the purchase, the lad spent the money by going to the theatre. It was stated that the prisoner had been previously brought up for thefts ; and his father gave him a very bad character, remarking that he could not keep his son at work and he would sleep oat at nights for weeks at a time—The Bench imposed a fine of 20s, or one month's imprisonment.

div.head: PAINFUL DROWNING CASE
div.p: PAINFUL DROWNING CASE

A painful drowning case occurred near Warrington on Tuesday evening. A young man named Thos. Warburton, nineteen years of age, son of John Warburton, foreman tanner, of ffl, Mersey-street, was walking out with Miss Mary Vernon, to whom he was engaged to be married, and when near the feeder that connects the branches of the Bridgewater Canal in the neighbaurhood of Dobson's locks. the young woman became frightened by the approach of a horse that was dragging a canal boat, She stepped on one side and fell into the feeder., which is about four feet wide and very rapid. In doing so she pulled her sweetheart with her. Their united cries for assistance attracted the atten- of the man in charge of the boat, and he succeeded in res- cuing Vernon after she had sunk twice. Warburton, who had made strenuous efforts to save his sweetheart, was carried away by the force of the stream and drowned. His body was recovered some hours afterwards, and was re- moved to the house of his brother In Latchford.

_ An inquest, respecting the occurrence was held at the Cheshire Cheese Inn, Latchford, on Thursday, before Mr. H. I Yates, coroner. The father of the deceased, John Warbur- ton, deposed that he was a foreman tanner, employed at Reynolds'a tannery. The deceased, who was 18 years old last May, was also a tanner and lived in the same house with him. He knew that his son was engaged to be married to Sarah Vernon. At about half-past seven on Tuesday night he left home well and hearty' but witness I did not know where he was going. Witness, heard of his I son's death from a brother-in-law of Sarah Vernon, at about 930 the same evening, and went to the feeder where the ac- cident happened, but did not see the body discovered-- Sarah Vernon, 137, hiersey-street, said that elm was engaged to be married to the deceased. On the night in question he came to where she lived, and they went for a walk together on the side of the canal. They crossed the turnbridge at Latchford, and then reached the road that runs along side the feeder. They passed a cauple of horses on the canal bank before they got to the feeder, and subsequently they heard the horses approaching behind them. She was frightened, and said to deceased, ." There are acme horses coming, let us step on one side." He had his arm around her at the time, and said, "Don't be afraid, we are all right here." She stepped a little on one side, thinking that she was stepping on to ground covered with grass, but the ground had been washed away, and she fell into the feeder. Deceased, who still had his arm round her, went in at the same time. ' She did not remember seeing him in the water, but did remember feeling his coat. Her cries for help had apparently attracted the at- tention of the boatmen in charge of the horses, for they came to the spot and dragged her out of the water by the hair. She was taken to the house at the locks. In answer to the coroner witness said that no blame was attached to anyone but herself and the deceased ; it was simply their own mistake and misfortune. The night was dark, If she had remained where deceased told her the accident would not have occurred. She was sure that the rope of the boat did not touch her, nor was there any carelessness on the part of the men in charge of the horses.—A county police-officer stated that the watch of the deceased had stopped at 8.75, about an hour after deceased and his sweetheart had left Mersev-street.—The jury returned a verdict of " accidental death."—The road on which the young man and woman were walking is a private one,passengers only being allowed to use it by sufferance, and no liability attaches to the Bridgewater Navigation Company.—Much commiseration is felt for the family of the young man and the bereaved young woman.

SETTLING AN AMAMI' CASX OET Or COMT.—George Rains, of Sutton. was summoned at the St. Helens Town '.Hall on Friday, for assaulting his wife Ann Rains, on the. 11th inst. The case was adjourned until Monday, when it again came on before Messrs W. Blinkhorn and C. J. Bishop. The complainant did not appear. and the defend- ant stated that the case bad been settled. The Clerk Fetid the woman bad had a summons granted to her free, and at least she might have come to the court and said that the case was settled--The Chairman (to the defend- ant): It is very unsatisfactory to the court after the woman has come here and told her tale and had a summons granted to her free to pay no attention to it now. (After a Pause) a summons will be Thsued for your wife to come here on Friday next. If she fails to obey that witness iummons a warrant will be issued for 'net' to be brought here forcibly.

ON THURSDAY evening next a tea party will be held in connection with Christ Church, Padgate. WARRINGTON HIGHWAY BoAaa.—A general meeting of ; this Board was held at the surveyor's office, in Sankey-street, i on Wednesday afternoon. The business was of a routine I character and not of public interest. i WESLEYAN TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.—On Tuesday evening ' a public meeting will be held under the auspices of the above Society in Bold.street school-room. The meeting is ' to be addressed by Sir William Fox, ex-Premier of New I Zealand ; by Mr. J. H. Raper, and other gentlemen. A MEDICAL STUDENT IN A DILEMMA —At the Borough I Court, on Thursday, a cripple named Thomas Bland, whose eyes were blackened, was charged with being drunk in Ken- drick-street the previous evening. It appeared that he I had been causing annoyance at the infirmary, and was , given into custody.—Dr. Joseph attended and said that the I prisoner stated that he was a medical student, and from a conversation that witness had had with him he judged that I to be correct. He had some medical knowledge. Wit- ness believed him to be suffering from the effects of drink. Prisoner had said that be was subject to epileptic fits' and no doubt that was so; probably he had fallen and hurt him- himself when in a fit. He (the doctor) did not see any traces of insanity about him, and hits. explanation seemed satisfactory—that he thought he knew Dr. Richmond, and wanted to secure a bed, as he was destitute.—Prisoner said that he fell asleep in the train and came to Warrington by mistake. He wished to go to his mother and sheers in Cumberland, to whom he had written for money. He had relations at New Brighton, whom he might go ta—lajer Litton, the presiding magistrate, gave instructions for pri- soner's fare to be paid to New Brighton. THOUGHT Reim/ea.—Mr. Alexander Scottarepeated on Saturday evening last in the Public Hall the exhibition of his extraordinary powers as a "thought reader." Mr. Alderman Holmes presided, and introduced Mr. Scott to the audience with a few pertinent remarks on the subject of the ! evening's entertainment, the new faculty being one which he considered, as did many eminent men of the clay, ought to be thoroughly investigated in view of its being made to I subserve if possible some useful purpose. A committee of gentlemen—amongst whom were Mr George Woods, Mr Dinwiddie, Mr George Riley, and Mr ilesket'n were ap- pointed by the audience to see that the various " tests " were made under proper conditions. Mr Scott went through I the wonderful exhibitions of his occult power with, perhaps, , greater success than on the previous evening, his fit et per- formance of locating an imaginary plan in each member of the committee being successful in every instance. In ad- dition to divining the number of a bank note, Mr Scott suc- cessfully inscribed on the black-board a short sentence of I three words present to the mind of a medium, whose thoughts Mr. Scott was supposed to be reading. Consider- able enthusiasm was manifested daring the application of the numerous tests. THE NEW BELLS AT THE PARISH CHURCII.—On Sunday offertories were taken at three services in the Parish Church in aid of the fund for paying the cast ot repairing the bells at the church. As has been previously stated, two new bells have been presented to the Parish Church to complete the peal of eight, and as it was found necessary to repair the old bells, that wotk has been done, and the offer- tories on Sunday went to help to pay the expense of those repairs. In the morning the sermon was preached by the Rev. W. G. Longden from the text, "Their sound is gone out unto all lands, and their words unto the end of the world." In the afternoon the sermon was preached by the Rev. R. W. P. Montgomery, and in the evening by the Rev. J. Weller' whose text was, " 0 worship the Lord in the beauty of holiness." After the sermon the following special prayer was offered up by the Rev. J. Weller, viz : ' Al- mighty Gad, who by the mouth of Thy servant Moses didst command to make two silver trumpets for the convocetion of solemn assemblies, be pleased to accept our offering of two more bells, and grant that throegh this generation, and through those which are to come, they may help continually to call together Thy faithful people to this house of prayer, to praise and worship Thy Holy-Name, through Jesus Christ Out Lord. Amen." The service was then concluded in the usual way. WICLIVVE CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH. ---. On Sunday evening the Reet. J. Yonge preached his usual monthly ser- mon to young men in the above church. The subject of his address was " Christian brotherhood ; its aims and ad- vantages ;" and he took as his text Timothy ii., part of the 22nd verse, " Follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace, with them that cell on the Lord out of a pure heart." To- wards the end of his discourse Mr. Yonge referred to the proposed formation of a Young Men's Guild in connection with that place of worship. Having spoken of the difficulty of leading a truly Christian life, he said the advantage of Christian fellowship and brotherhood was to render that lifeless difficult. The objects at the proposed guild were to furnish a bond of Christian Brotherhood and to promote the personal well-being and mutual helpfulness of its mem- bers. A room was to be provided for the members where they might resort in their evenings for suitable conversa- tion, reading, and enjoyment. Meetings for prayer would be held, and the members would be encouraged to care for one another in trouble and sickness. But the central idea of the whole thing was that upon which he had been trying to speak that night—Christian brotherhood. They desired to provide a Christian society for their young men, to seek pure intelligent religious society. Ita conclusion, be asked not only for the adhesion of all the young men, but for the hearty powerful sympathy of all of their Wycliffe people. There was a large attendance at the service. THE GRAND CLOTHING HALL COISIPANY.—There has re- cently been on view in the window of the Grand Clothing Hall Company, Bridge-street, a splendid illuminated ad- dress encased in handsonee bindings, and an elaborate and costly cabinet, which are to be presented to Mr. I. Hart, the head of the company, in honour of his having been elected Mayor of Leicester. These presents have been sub- scribed for by the employas of the company at the branch establishments at Waerington, Sheffield, Preston, Rochdale, Derby, and Burton. The cabinet bears the inscription on a silver plate :—"Presented to his worship Israel Hart, E-q., Mayor of Leicester, by his ernaloyes at the branch es- tablishments;" and the address runs as follows :--" Dear Sire—We, the undersignen, wishing to congratulate you upon having been elected to the high and honourable office of Mayor of Leicester, beg your acceptance of this teatime.. trial as a token of our gratification of the event. We alio ' wish to convey to you our feelings of respect and pleasure upon this auspicious occasion, and ask your acceptance of the accompanying gift as a token of our appreciation of the many superior qualities which have endeared you to your employ6s and fellow-townsmen. We trust your dear wife and family may enjoy with you long life and health, and further that you may be long spared to render other important services to the inhabitants of Leiceeter.—Signed by T. M. Mee, B. Dennis, C. Lane, W. Hurrah, G. Emitter- son, and C. Purkie, on behalf of the subscribers." A, BRUTAL HUSBAND. AND FATHER.—Yesterday, at the Borough Court, William Caldwelt, Harts-place, Bridge- street, was charged on a warrant with assaulting his wife on Wednesday.—MT. P. Davies, who appeared for complainant. described the assault as baying been a very serious one. The wife, he said, was a hard-working woman, who had long maintained her husband, who spent his days in bed, drinking with his wife's money at nights. On the day in question he was thrashing one of the children, which be threatened to kill, and on the mother interfering he struck her violently on the face and- bead, tried to throw her down- stairs, and said that- he would "swing for her." She was rendered almost insensible by his violence.—Complainant spoke to the assault, and said t hat she had on ether occasions been ill-treated by prisoner, who, she added, knocked the children about, 'and gave one of them a black eye They bad been married- nine years and hid four. children. Chief Constable Hunt said that Sirs. Caldwell came to see him after the assault, at which time she bore traces of having been badly trreated.—P.C. Chentler stated that when apprehended prisoner said that he would make his wife "Sit up" for It.—The Mayor described- the defence of the prisoner, who said his wife struck him and has gave her a "clout," as a tissue of falsehoods, deliberately invented. To describe him as a brute was almost using too good a word. He would be sent to prison for ten weeks and a separate mainten- ance order would be granted the wife, and prisoner to conZ tribute IN a week, and she to have the custody of the children.

SIR STAFFORD NORTEICOTE AT BARNSTAPLE:Sir Staf- ford Northcote addressed a meeting on Monday night, at Barnetaple, in connection with his forthcoming candidature for the new division of the county. He said that Conserva- tives accepted the addition to the electorate without fear that those enfranchised would maks a bad use of their power. After condemning the foreign, colonial, and Irish policy of the Government, he said it was never more impor- tant to maintain and develop the strength of the colonies than at the present time. Their statesmen, instead of tak- ing pains to preserve the respect of the Empire. were intent only upon saving, themselves from responsibility. It was their duty to maintain the greatness and unity of the Em- pire, and their position as an Eastern and oceanic Power, and to make it evident to the colonists that we have their Interests at heart, regarded them as an integral part of the Empire, and were not prepared to sacrifice them to un- reasonable demands on the part of other countries, or to bring them into foreign difficulties by neglecting at the !proper moment,to deal with questions that affected foreign nations. He expressed a fear lest harm might be done amongst the new electors by Socialist doctrines.--On Tues- day, continuieg his electioneering tour, Sir Stafford North- cote addreseed the members of a Working Men's Conserva- tive Association and also a publit meeting. He expressed the opiniort that Liberalism was at low water at the present, and that the Conservative party would again come forth and maintain the position it formerly held. In reference to the agitatioreon colonial affairs,,he said we lead contracted obli- gations which we could not withdraw from without dis- honour and discredit to ourselves. There would be a good deal of discussion in Parliament on colonial questions. Sir Staffmetonce More repeated himself respecting the concert of Europe, declaring thathe Liberals were no more anxious to maintain that concert. than the Conservatives, and that the :Atter were more successful in the effort than their op- ponents. At the prt:sent time, he said, they never took up their paper without fearand trembling as to what might be tholatest development of the Egyptian question. Tba Khartoum exped3ion could bring upon the Government of , this country nothing but shame and confusion. Toucleing domestic affaira the right hon. Baronet said that nanuty government and other matters would be dealt with by the new Parliaratst. On Wednesday night, Sir Stafford North- cote spoke at Ilfracombe. He deprecated the gloomy pro- phecies uttered in some quarters as to the possible results of the eeform measures. He thought, however, that the depres- sion in the country demanded a careful inquiry, and that it was the duty of statesmen to see in what direction our com- mercial eyetem required amendment.
